item.title: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction; Nasdaq erases 2026 gain as AI rout picks up steam
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.

The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.

Anthropic lost 8.5%, giving back a large chunk of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid more than 13% and around 14%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. It also recorded its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.

Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each lost more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.

"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."

The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.

On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.

Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.

For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-20 23:46 UTC

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/stock-market-today-live-updates.html

item.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test

- Published

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-20 23:28 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jre8xd83qgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

- Published

The livestream begins.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

170 carcasses found

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."

In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."

'God knows what was inside those urns'

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Or not, as the case may be.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT â but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law â estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them â and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (Â£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.…

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-20 23:20 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn502ek17yvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Man accused of sparking deadly Los Angeles wildfire found guilty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The 30-year-old accused of sparking the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles was found guilty of two federal arson charges in a Friday verdict that came months after his first trial concluded with a hung jury.

For two weeks, a fresh batch of jurors listened to prosecutors mount their case against Jonathan Rinderknecht.

They argued the former Uber driver was responsible for the January 2025 wildfire, which claimed 12 lives and devastated the Pacific Palisades, an affluent enclave on the California coast.

Rinderknecht, in prosecutors’ account, used a lighter to set a brush fire in the hillside area. The state cast him as a disgruntled young man who sought retribution against the world for personal gripes, including failed romances, and perceived societal injustices like wealth inequality.

Firefighters suppressed the so-called Lachman brush fire last January, but its embers simmered underground, before being swept by powerful winds and erupting above ground into the Palisades inferno that destroyed thousands of homes and businesses.

Rinderknecht had maintained his innocence, pleading not guilty to the revised charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

For the retrial, jurors were instructed explicitly to not consider the adequacy of the fire department’s response to the Lachman and Palisades blaze. The department has faced criticism for failing to fully extinguish the Lachman fire that eventually reignited.

The note came after some of the first trial’s jurors were wary of pinning the blame squarely on Rinderknecht, citing the fire department’s past actions. Of that deadlocked panel, two voted for guilty, while 10 others were not convinced.

Rinderknecht’s defense team also doubled down during the retrial on an alternative explanation for the Palisades fire, suggesting the initial brush blaze was ignited by fireworks.

Prosecutors dismissed the theory as “baseless” in a court filing where they raised concern over the reliability and late introduction of a defense witness, whose testimony would reference stains at a private residence that supposedly indicated fireworks had been discharged.

Rinderknecht will be sentenced on 17 March.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-20 23:20 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/los-angeles-palisades-wildfire-trial-verdict

item.title: Republican senator blocks Trump pick to lead cybersecurity agency who denied US Capitol was attacked on January 6 – live
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Republican senator blocks Trump pick to lead cybersecurity agency who denied US Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is about to be replaced by a Democrat, told multiple news outlets that he has blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the federal government’s cybersecurity and infrastructure security agency (Cisa), Michael LoSapio, one day after the nominee denied that the US Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.

Tillis, who elected not to run for re-election without Trump’s support, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination, which will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.

Tillis previously told a reporter for Punchbowl on Thursday that he would use the procedural move to delay a vote on LoSapio’s confirmation before Democrats take power in January.

At his Senate confirmation hearing on Thursday, LoSapio, the chief information security officer for Palantir, a technology firm founded by JD Vance’s mentor, Peter Thiel, was asked by senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, “Was there an attack on the Capitol of January 6 2021?”

After initially replying, “I don’t know,” LoSapio said, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”

The agency LoSapio was nominated by Trump to lead, Cisa, plays a role in protecting US elections infrastructure from hacking.

The week after the 2020 election, as Trump falsely claimed that count had been rigged, Cisa was one of a number of federal agencies with oversight of election infrastructure to issue a statement calling the election “the most secure in American history” and noting that there was “no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised.”

After he returned to the White House last year, Trump signed an April 2025 presidential memorandum directing executive offices to take steps to address supposed “risks from Chris Krebs,” who lead Cisa in 2020. “Krebs, through CISA, falsely and baselessly denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen, including by inappropriately and categorically dismissing widespread election malfeasance and serious vulnerabilities with voting machines,” Trump’s memorandum claimed.

Source: The Guardian US | Published: 2026-11-20 23:16 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/20/donald-trump-brooke-rollins-religion-sean-cairncross-senate-alaska-white-house-press-conference-us-politics-latest-news-updates

item.title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US

- Published

A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.

The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.

Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.

Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.

Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.

"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.

The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.

Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.

The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.

Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.

Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.

New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.

At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.

Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

Source: BBC Science & Environment | Published: 2026-11-20 22:57 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4gn0dg9194o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

But bleach can't conquer per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—commonly called PFAS—a class of synthetic chemicals. Resistant to grease and water, they gave us nonstick cookware, waterproofing technology, durable medical devices and firefighting foam. But these substances' ironclad chemical bonds, which earned them the nickname "forever chemicals," have a darker side linked to deadly cancers, infertility, and immune and developmental damage to infants and children.

They might also be called "everywhere chemicals" because they are widely found in basic items like clothes, cosmetics and pizza boxes, as well as soil, air and drinking water.

"PFAS—this guy doesn't care about anything," said Ashburton plant manager Mohammed Almafrachi, Ph.D. '26, as he led the UMD students through the facility last Tuesday. "We can add whatever chemicals we want to the water, but he's going to stay here."

A research partnership targets PFAS

Not if Guangbin Li, UMD assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering, has anything to say about it. Although one government study detected PFAS chemicals in nearly half of the nation's tap water, the PFAS expert envisions a day when the stubborn chemicals can be curbed to the point of eliminating health risks.

For the past two years, he and his students have collaborated with Baltimore's Department of Public Works, which oversees the city's water system, to study PFAS interventions; city officials have provided water samples and data to Li's team, while he has shared his technology with water engineers.

"People call it forever chemicals, but scientifically it's not forever," Li said. "We still have a ways to go, but we have the technology to destroy them."

A sponge for stubborn chemicals

While many scientists have attempted to lower PFAS by converting it with aggressive heat or electricity to carbon dioxide—nontoxic, but still a gas that contributes to climate change—Li's method uses micrometer-sized adsorbents like carbon that soak the PFAS up like a sponge and lock it in place. The resulting solids either remain safely buried in soil for years or can be removed from treated water after a few hours to a few days.

By experimenting with different chemical combinations with which to arm the adsorbents, Li's aim is to build a kind of super sponge that ensnares not one but the majority of the most dangerous PFAS and converts them into recyclable materials.

At the same time, his research has led him to question the promises of other scientists using similar methods. While some claim that current soil-based adsorbents can trap certain PFAS for up to 100 years, Li has found that the true number could be less than 20 years.

"We should be prepared for a future of these chemicals coming back to us sooner than we think," said Li, who recently published his findings in Environmental Science & Technology.

Bringing lab research to Baltimore's plants

The Ashburton plant, a large, labyrinthine building erected in 1956, processes up to 165 million gallons (625 million liters) of drinking water a day for consumers stretching from Towson to Columbia, Maryland, but it was never designed to treat PFAS. Li is working with Almafrachi—his former student who runs the Ashburton facility as well as the city's other two filtration plants—to identify opportunities for modifications and pilot programs introducing new adsorbents.

"He has all the scientific and engineering knowledge of PFAS, and we have the operational knowledge," said Almafrachi, who as a UMD doctoral student designed a chemical catalyst that adsorbs PFAS. He calls the collaboration between the university and his team "Terps helping Terps."

Meanwhile, through his connections to Almafrachi and other Baltimore engineers, Li appreciates the chance to expose his students to the real-world infrastructure challenges facing the city, which houses one of the nation's oldest filtration systems.

"We have fancy technology in our lab, but it's still a lab," he says. "There's a gap, sometimes huge, between it and the real, full-scale system that students see on the tour."

Publication details

Liu Jiang et al., Biological Aging as an Overlooked Factor Controlling the Effectiveness of Colloidal Activated Carbon for PFAS Removal in Subsurface Environments, Environmental Science & Technology (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.6c06602

Journal information: Environmental Science & Technology

Provided by University of Maryland

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-20 22:40 UTC

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemicals-dont.html

item.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

That's according to new research on a species of fish called blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) recently published in Communications Biology. The study was co-led by Alec Lackmann, Ph.D., a fisheries research scientist from the Swenson College of Science and Engineering at the University of Minnesota Duluth (UMD), Luke Holmquist, a Missouri River fisheries biologist with Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews, Ph.D., a fisheries biologist with the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa.

Native to 23 states, including Minnesota and Montana, the blue sucker is categorized as imperiled in 22 of them. Population data over three decades from Montana have shown virtually no small (young) blue suckers coming into the population, suggesting recruitment failure possibly due to habitat fragmentation caused by large dams.

"For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range," said the researchers. "Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap." Those researchers wanted to find out more about the species by examining the age structure, recruitment trends and longevity using recently refined aging techniques.

Tiny earstones reveal unexpected ages

From 2023 to 2026, the team thoughtfully collected and processed samples of close to 50 fish from a population in Montana to learn more. What they found is completely rewriting our understanding of the species and adds to a growing group of fish that were previously underappreciated but have lifespans often greater than those of human beings.

To precisely age the fish, scientists extract what are called the otoliths, or earstones, from inside the cranium of the fish and then thinly section the stones to determine their age.

Approximately 97% of fish species have otoliths. They're tiny, stone-like structures that grow throughout the fish's lifetime, forming a new layer each year. When processed properly, scientists can examine the otolith with a compound microscope and count the layers, like the rings on a tree, and learn the age of the fish. When Lackmann and his partners found the data from the otoliths to far exceed previous estimates, they then set out to test the validity of the otolith ages.

Lackmann, an expert and pioneer in otolith aging and validation techniques, started on the project in 2023, after fisheries colleagues in Montana had noticed long-term trends that suggested there weren't many new generations of the fish. "Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them," Lackmann said.

In these otoliths from fish previously thought to live to about 40 years, "we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old," he said. "When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity."

A nuclear signature confirms the ages

To confirm what they were seeing in the microscope was accurate, they used bomb radiocarbon dating, testing the otolith ages both within and across individuals against the known increase in atmospheric radiocarbon levels that came from the widespread nuclear bomb testing in the mid-20th century.

"Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid- to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere," said Lackmann. "This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you're able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate.

"Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that's where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker."

A growing list of centenarian fish

Lackmann's research has previously redefined the paradigm for several other freshwater fish species through improved aging techniques (bigmouth buffalo 2019, 2024), and documented environmental conditions related to sporadic recruitment success in North Dakota (2021) and Canada (2023, 2025 ), and his team's 2023 study published in Scientific Reports found the second genus of animal ever for which three or more species (buffalofishes) have known lifespans greater than 100 years.

This latest study makes the blue sucker the fourth centenarian catostomid (sucker) fish discovered (all since 2019), joining bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo and black buffalo, and recognizes the blue sucker as one of the oldest-living vertebrates in North America.

"To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank—it's just wild," said Holmquist. "We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river."

Publication details

Alec R. Lackmann et al., Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA, Communications Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3

Journal information: Communications Biology , Scientific Reports

item.title: Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Wylie, D., Arasappan, D., Ross, D., Hyde, T. M., Ressler, K. J., Kleinman, J. E., Weinberger, D. R., Daskalakis, N. P., Nemeroff, C. B., & Champagne, F. A. (2026). DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

They cover AI, engineering, materials science, cybersecurity, space, games, online communities, and any shiny new technology that catches their eye. She has written for Science News, Scientific American, Nature, Washington Post, Guardian, Chemical & Engineering News, IEEE Spectrum, and others. They also write science-fiction and fantasty. The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.

The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials. Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.

But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

item.title: Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

New research suggests health officials may be overselling the protective power of the annual flu shot—but that doesn't mean folks should skip it, researchers added. The new analysis finds the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness against infection that's routinely stated, according to researchers from the University of Maryland.

In many seasons, it may not even match current circulating strains, they noted.

"The 40% to 60% range may describe some seasons, but it doesn't adequately reflect the variability we see over time," said study senior author Dr. Justin Ortiz, a researcher at the university's Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health.

The trick, he said, is "to communicate that uncertainty without losing sight of the substantial benefits of vaccination."

The findings were recently published in JAMA Network Open.

In the study, Ortiz's team looked at end-of-season estimates of flu vaccine effectiveness for flu seasons from 2004 to 2005 through 2023 to 2024. They also looked at whether a particular season's vaccine was well matched to the flu strains that actually appeared.

The team found that influenza vaccines had a median effectiveness of 39.5% in preventing flu infection. That's below the 40% to 60% effectiveness range typically cited by public health officials and media, researchers noted. (Median means some years' protection was greater and some years' less.)

They noted that higher estimates of effectiveness are often predicated on the notion that the flu vaccine is a good match for circulating strains of the virus. However, the study showed it often wasn't the case: In 11 of the 18 tracked seasons, vaccines did not match circulating strains.

None of this means flu shots are useless, and Ortiz's team stressed that shots are still the most effective means Americans have of preventing influenza, which kills between 6,300 and 52,000 people each year, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

And this year, flu is spreading early, accounting for 2,100 deaths so far this season. The CDC estimates that, during the 2023 to 2024 flu season, vaccination saved 7,900 lives. It also prevented 120,000 flu-related hospitalizations and 9.8 million flu-related illnesses.

It's hoped the new data will help spur research into improving influenza vaccines so they offer broader protection against the ever-mutating virus.

"The message is clear that annual flu shots remain our best option for now as we continue to develop vaccines that provide more predictable and lasting protection," said study lead author Dr. Matthew Wolpert, an internal medicine resident at the University of Maryland Medical Center.

Publication details

Matthew D. Wolpert et al., Testing the 40% to 60% Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Heuristic, JAMA Network Open (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.42906

Journal information: JAMA Network Open

item.title: Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Frustrated that your cholesterol levels aren't budging for the better? You may have your genes to blame, a new study finds.

Researchers at Stanford University found certain genes influenced, for good or ill, how women's bodies dealt with cholesterol.

It's an issue plaguing millions of health-conscious Americans.

"We have people who come into clinic and say, 'I changed my diet and it made no difference in my cholesterol.' Or they say, 'I changed my diet and it had a huge effect on my cholesterol,'" noted senior author Dr. Shoa Clarke, a cardiologist and assistant professor of medicine and pediatrics at Stanford Medicine.

His team's findings are not meant to deter folks from fighting cholesterol, however.

"Sometimes people think, 'Oh, if I'm genetically prone to something, then it doesn't really matter what my diet is or what the environment is like; it's genetically predetermined.' But what we're saying here is the opposite," Clarke said in a news release. "The people who had this genetic predisposition for higher LDL ['bad' cholesterol] were actually the ones with the most sensitivity to diet, where diet has the best chance of helping them—or hurting them, if the diet is not good."

The findings were published Nov. 18 in the journal JACC: Advances.

The new study looked at data collected for decades among more than 21,000 American women, as part of the ongoing Women's Health Initiative.

At the study's beginning in 1991, the women's median age was 65, meaning half were younger and half were older. About half were White, a third were Black and 15% were Hispanic.

All checked in regularly with detailed reports on their daily diet, and all of the women got regular cholesterol checks.

Most importantly for this study, the women also underwent complex genetic analysis.

The Stanford team found that certain genes seem to predispose women to higher levels of cholesterol, and that was especially true for women who consumed high levels of unhealthy saturated fats. For women lacking these genes, no such association was found.

Further research showed that women who ranked in the top 25% in terms of a genetic propensity for high LDL cholesterol and saturated fat intake were also much more prone to suffer a stroke or heart attack.

The other 75% (with a less pronounced genetic predisposition) did not seem as affected by saturated fat intake, the team noted.

"We found the same thing—that the association between saturated fat intake and risk for having cardiovascular events was amplified for those people at the upper end of the genetic spectrum," Clarke said. "This variation in response to saturated fat may be one of the reasons there is so much controversy and disagreement over how much is OK in a diet."

The study is in line with guidelines from the World Health Organization urging people to limit their intake of red meat, because it contains high levels of saturated fat.

Clarke's team found that—despite what fans of high-fat ketogenic diets might claim—higher saturated fat intake offered no protective effect for the heart, even among those at relatively low genetic risk for higher LDL cholesterol.

"The effects of saturated fat may not be the same for everyone, but there isn't any evidence of a cardiovascular benefit to eating more saturated fat," Clarke said. "The harms might vary from small to large depending on who you are."

In prior research, the Stanford group created a "polygenic risk score" assessing an individual's relative odds for poor heart health based on their genetics.

"We don't yet have evidence that polygenic risk scores should be used to guide diet recommendations," Clarke said. "But that certainly is a future area of study, and from what our results in this new study suggest, could indeed be a fruitful one."

More information

Alexa Barad et al., Association Between Saturated Fat Intake and Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Across the Genetic Spectrum, JACC: Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.103423

item.title: Democrats Demand Answers From Oz After Delay in $50B Rural Health Awards
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Democrats Demand Answers From Oz After Delay in $50B Rural Health Awards

Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.

Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”

Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.

Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.

In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.

The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.

“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.

CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.

Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.

That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.

Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.

Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”

Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.

The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”

After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.

Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.

Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.

The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”

Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.

In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.

It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.

In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.

“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

item.title: Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

The study found that body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs), as they are known, can be a significant source of distress, particularly among young people who also experienced anxiety, depression and bullying.

Researchers asked more than 5,400 school students ages 11 to 18, mainly in Oxfordshire and Liverpool, questions about BFRBs as part of the larger OxWell Student Survey. Those who had experienced BFRBs were asked to what extent those behaviors upset or distressed them, ranging from 'not at all' to 'a great deal."

The data, published in BMJ Mental Health, showed:

- In the sample, 58.5% of young people reported at least one BFRB.

- These behaviors were a significant source of distress for 13% (answering that they caused 'quite a lot' or 'a great deal' of distress or upset).

- The most commonly reported behavior was nail biting (43.6%), followed by skin picking (31.3%) and hair pulling (14.5%), with 17.6% of those experiencing BFRBs reporting two or more.

- Hair pulling and skin picking were associated with substantially higher levels of distress than nail biting (37% and 29%, respectively, versus 11%).

- Girls and transgender/gender-diverse young people were substantially more likely than boys both to experience BFRBs and to find them distressing. Around one in four transgender/gender-diverse young people and one in six girls reported distressing BFRBs, compared with around one in 18 boys.

- More than a third of young people with anxiety and depression (34%) had experienced distressing BFRBs, as well as 27% of those who had experienced bullying.

The researchers also found that distressing BFRBs were reported by around one in five young people who identified as autistic or having ADHD—approximately twice the rate seen in those without these conditions. This difference was largely explained by higher levels of emotional distress and experiences of bullying, rather than neurodivergence itself.

Lead author professor Clare Mackay from the University of Oxford's Department of Psychiatry, who has experienced BFRBs herself, said, "These findings show that BFRBs are common in adolescents, and that they are strongly associated with emotional distress and social adversity. This distress often goes unrecognized because these types of behaviors are rarely discussed in schools, health care or wider society, and so those experiencing them often have little support.

"BFRBs aren't simply bad habits. They're often signs that a young person is struggling. Asking whether someone ever pulls, picks or bites at themselves in a way that upsets them could open an important conversation. If we recognize these behaviors earlier, we have a much better chance of offering support before they become entrenched."

Co-author professor Polly Waite, deputy director of the Oxford Centre for Emerging Minds Research and co-lead for the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Oxford Health's Mental Health in Development Theme, said, "This research highlights the need for better support for young people with BFRBs. Shame and stigma can make it difficult for young people to talk about these behaviors or seek help. We need to open up conversations about BFRBs, challenge the stigma surrounding them, and help young people realize they are not alone."

The data came from the OxWell Student Survey, which is conducted every two years. The findings are shared back with schools to inform policy and practice, as well as with local authorities to guide education and mental health provision, and to shape national policy on education and well-being.

The findings follow another recent qualitative study highlighting the central role of shame in young people who experience hair pulling. Twelve adolescents took part in semistructured interviews, which found that shame was an enduring emotion that triggered, maintained and exacerbated hair pulling. The findings were published in the journal Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice.

Publication details

Clare Mackay et al., Body-focused repetitive behaviours are common, distressing and under-recognised: a cross-sectional study from the OxWell Student Survey, BMJ Mental Health (2026). DOI: 10.1136/bmjment-2026-302871

Laura A. F. Lee et al., Tangled in shame: A qualitative exploration of shame in adolescent hairpulling, Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice (2026). DOI: 10.1111/papt.70114

Journal information: BMJ Mental Health

item.title: ICE detention of Princeton scientist rattles academia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to The New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.

The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences to present new research and network with colleagues may be too risky during a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.

“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students on visas to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, a John Hopkins academic who said a staff member of hers was detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of U.S. conferences have reported smaller attendance over the past two years, and some have considered hosting in other countries.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”

Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained. In one notable instance, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE last year in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school, wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. A third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.

“I think it speaks to how exceptional of a researcher Eva is that she can work on projects that really span multiple disciplines, that require that she go and learn the foundations, not just of AI and machine learning, and not just computational models of the brain, but also understanding how do you run the experiment on the mice. She’s in the lab actually doing the surgery on the mice, gathering the data from the mice, analyzing those data, and running the AI experiments,” said Benjamin Eysenbach, a computer scientist at Princeton and one of Xie’s advisers.

As an example of the respect she commands among peers, Eysenbach cited a workshop she convened at last year’s NeurIPS conference, one of the premiere machine learning conferences. Xie presented research of her own, and also brought together leaders in AI and in neuroscience to see how they could collaborate.

It was an opportunity both to “introduce these important questions about the brain to folks in AI that might be equipped with new methods, and to help folks working on neuroscience questions define what are the right AI tools,” Eysenbach said.

Krithik Ramesh, a fellow researcher, is among those who has benefitted from her guidance. The two had overlapped at science fair competitions throughout high school, and when Ramesh was considering transferring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie had completed her undergraduate degree, he turned to her for counsel. He learned about Xie’s detention after a friend saw a post on social media. His immediate reaction was disbelief, followed by a sense of unmooring as a fellow researcher.

“We academics exist for the benefit of the public,” he said. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people. That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.”

Source: STAT | Published: 2026-11-20 21:19 UTC

Original link: https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/20/princeton-researcher-eva-yi-xie-ice-detention-rattles-interational-scholars/?utm_campaign=rss

item.title: Smartlook Alternative for WordPress: Self-Hosted Session Recordings and Heatmaps
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

We build Opti-Behavior, a WordPress plugin; this guide was first published on our blog. The export steps and the checklist are useful whatever tool you pick.

Smartlook stopped selling new subscriptions on 31 May 2026 and the platform will be switched off on 30 September 2027, with all remaining data deleted. If your recordings and heatmaps run on Smartlook, you need a Smartlook alternative before your paid plan ends, and you need to export what you want to keep first. This guide gives the official dates, the export route Smartlook documents, a checklist to compare replacements, and the steps to move a WordPress site to a self-hosted tool.

The short version: copy your data with the Smartlook APIs before your paid subscription expires, list what you really use (recordings, heatmaps, funnels, events), then test one or two replacements on a real page for a week before your plan runs out.

When Smartlook stops: the dates

Smartlook has joined Cisco and will wind down as a standalone product. Its features move to Digital Experience Analytics inside Splunk Observability Cloud. The official timeline, published on the Smartlook pricing page (read on 11 November 2026), is:

- 31 May 2026, End of Sale: no new Smartlook subscriptions are sold.

- 31 August 2026, End of Contract Renewals: no renewals or expansions for existing accounts.

- 31 August 2027, Last Day of Support: all remaining paid subscriptions end.

- 30 September 2027, Platform Decommissioned: the platform is switched off and all remaining customer data is deleted.

Between the end of your paid plan and 30 September 2027, Smartlook says you can still use its Free plan, with that plan's limits. Smartlook also states that Splunk will not migrate historical data from Smartlook to Digital Experience Analytics, and that your current subscription will not be transitioned automatically.

In practice, the date that matters for you is not 2027. It is the day your own paid plan ends: after it, you lose the paid features and work inside free-plan limits. Write that date down now and plan the switch a few weeks before it.

Export your Smartlook data before the shutdown

Smartlook's official advice, on the same pricing page FAQ, is to export the data you wish to retain before your paid subscription expires, and in any case no later than 31 August 2027. It says you can create a copy of your data using the Smartlook APIs, and it points to four export resources:

- Smartlook Reports and Exports (help centre)

- How to create a REST API token

- REST API Overview

- List of available REST API calls

For anything these pages do not cover, Smartlook asks customers to contact their Account Manager or support@smartlook.com. Before you start, decide what is worth keeping. Most teams do not need every old recording. They need:

- The list of events and funnels you defined, so you can rebuild them in the new tool.

- Reports you shared with clients or your team, as files.

- The few recordings that explain a known bug or a decision, saved with a note on why they matter.

Old behavior data ages fast. A redesign, a new theme or a new checkout makes last year's heatmaps less useful. Your event and funnel definitions keep their value, so export those first.

Checklist to choose a Smartlook alternative

Feature lists look alike, so compare replacements on the points that change your daily work and your costs. Ask each vendor these five questions and write the answers in one table.

1. Where is the data stored?

A hosted service keeps recordings on the vendor's servers. A self-hosted plugin keeps them in your own WordPress database and files. This decides who you list as a processor in your privacy policy, how long data is kept, and what happens to it if the vendor changes its offer, as Smartlook customers are seeing now.

2. What does the free quota really cover?

Check what is counted (sessions, page views, recordings), whether bots count, and what happens at the limit: does recording pause, does old data disappear, do features lock? A quota that sounds large can be used up by bot traffic on a small site.

3. How long is the trial, and does it need a card?

Two weeks rarely covers a full buying cycle. A longer trial lets you see weekend traffic, a campaign and a few real sales before you decide.

4. Does it understand WooCommerce?

If you sell with WooCommerce, check that the tool sees the steps product, cart, checkout and order without custom code, and that it can show where buyers leave.

5. What does it cost in page speed?

Do not trust a vendor's speed claim, ours included. Measure it: run PageSpeed Insights on the same page three times with the tool on, then three times with it off, and compare the median.

Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, Mouseflow and Opti-Behavior side by side

The table only lists facts published by each vendor on its own page. Plans and limits change, so open the source before you decide.

If your site is not on WordPress, a hosted tool is the simpler choice: Opti-Behavior is a WordPress plugin and only runs there. If you are on WordPress and want the recordings in your own database, read on.

Switch to Opti-Behavior on WordPress in 5 steps

Keep Smartlook running in parallel until your export is done and the new tool shows data.

- Install the Free plugin. In WordPress, go to Plugins → Add New, search "Opti-Behavior", or download it from wordpress.org.

- Activate it. No snippet to paste in your theme and no external account for the Free plugin.

- Let tracking run. Visits, pages, sources, click heatmaps and funnels start with the next visitors. If nothing shows after a few visits, a page cache is often serving an old page: purge it once.

- Start the Pro trial from the plugin. Click "Try Pro Free" in the plugin: 6 months of every Pro feature, no credit card. Then free up to 1,000 sessions a month (bots and spam included), with the data on your own server. At the quota, new Pro recordings pause; nothing is deleted.

- Read Smart Insights after the first visits. Open Smart Insights once a few dozen sessions are in. It lists what to look at first, so you do not have to watch recordings at random.

Then rebuild the funnels you exported from Smartlook. On a WooCommerce shop, the plugin suggests a purchase funnel (shop, product, cart, checkout, order received) that you create in one click.

From modules to a report that says what to fix

Collecting behavior data is the easy part. The hard part is finding the one problem worth fixing this week. Opti-Behavior connects its modules so that the answer comes to you instead of the other way round.

- Heatmaps show where visitors click (Free) and how far they scroll (Pro).

- Session recordings (Pro) show the visit behind a number.

- Funnels show the step where visitors leave (Free, with more in Pro).

- Form analytics (Pro) show the field where people give up.

- Shop counts product → cart → checkout → order on WooCommerce (Free); Pro adds the estimated amount lost per step and payment errors.

- Error tracking (Pro) logs JavaScript errors with the page and the date.

Smart Insights reads these modules together and turns them into findings: a funnel step that loses most visitors, a button nobody clicks, a form field that blocks. The core findings are Free; Smart Insights Pro adds the evidence from recordings, forms, errors, journeys, funnels, Shop and A/B tests.

The last step is a report you can act on. The short site report (Free) gives the traffic summary and the 3 most costly issues, each with what to do:

On a single page, Page X-Ray (Pro) goes further: it lists what to fix, most costly first, why it matters and what to do for each problem. You can print it or save it as a PDF to share with a client or a developer.

A simple routine works: once a week, open the report, fix the first issue, and check the same report seven days later to see whether the number moved.
