item.title: Overcoming Late-Stage Tech Interview Rejections and Market Stagnation Through Strategic Career Repositioning
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The 2026 engineering hiring bottleneck does not signal permanent industry decline or personal inadequacy among experienced builders. Instead, it reflects a structural employer-side arbitrage in which organizations demand Staff-level execution at Senior compensation—making late-stage rejections and prolonged searches an expected consequence of current hiring mechanics rather than proof of diminished competence. For senior engineers, remaining in a high-volume application loop or passively waiting for a return to 2020–2021 expansion carries real stakes: prolonged career stagnation, burnout, and permanent downward wage-to-skill compression. Positioning effectively requires shifting from volume-driven attrition to targeted, leverage-driven execution.

Late-Stage Rejection Mechanics in Multi-Round Loops

In a five-plus round hiring funnel, each stage operates as a sequential filter with non-zero false-negative probability. When per-round pass probability remains bounded below unity due to interviewer variance and rubric compression, compound pass probability across n independent stages decays exponentially as the product of p_i—even for strong candidates whose underlying capability is sound. Attrition is therefore built into the geometry of the funnel before a candidate's technical ceiling is ever tested in production.

In late-stage management or hiring-manager debriefs, evaluation logic frequently shifts from cumulative scoring to veto or strong-no gating. A single misaligned signal on stakeholder framing, ambiguity tolerance, or organizational fit overrides high technical signals from earlier rounds, producing late-stage rejections precisely when candidate time investment is highest.

- Asymmetric hiring risk -> conservative rubric thresholds -> high false-negative rate: Because a bad hire carries sustained payroll, onboarding, and team-drag cost while passing on a capable candidate incurs no immediate ledger penalty, evaluators raise passing thresholds toward near-perfection. As a result, the funnel filters out engineers whose performance would have cleared Staff+ bars during 2020–2021 expansion, turning risk avoidance into systematic false negatives.

- Compressed evaluation windows -> high variance in leadership signal -> management-round veto: Time-bounded interviews force inference of complex judgment and cross-functional influence from sparse samples. Sparse sampling amplifies disagreement among evaluators and makes late-stage management blocks routine, punishing strong candidates for noisy signal extraction rather than weak execution.

Intermediate conclusion: Late-stage rejections in multi-round loops are largely a product of multiplicative filter decay, asymmetric risk incentives, and high-variance late-stage veto gates—meaning a final-round "no" often measures committee caution and sample noise rather than a candidate's readiness to deliver.

Role Consolidation and Compensation Band Compression

Tighter capital efficiency and finite headcount approval cycles shift resource allocation from seat expansion to scope expansion per seat. Rather than opening new requisitions across layers, engineering organizations leave entry-level or redundant requisitions unfilled and concentrate operational, architectural, and cross-system ownership inside Senior requisitions.

Compensation structures operate under hard band ceilings and internal equity constraints. When role scope expands toward Staff-level expectations while leveling remains anchored to Senior bands, compensation does not scale linearly with acquired capability or prior seniority. Candidates with Staff+ signal either get mapped down into a capped Senior band or get rejected when expectations and band limits collide, creating a structural mismatch between what employers extract and what they pay for.

Intermediate conclusion: Role consolidation paired with rigid compensation bands creates an employer-side arbitrage: organizations capture broader architectural and cross-system scope inside Senior titles while holding pay and leveling to constrained bands.

Feedback Loop Instability and Fatalism

The candidate search operates as a closed feedback loop coupling external rejection signals with internal cognitive state and search strategy. Repeated late-stage failures after multi-round loops increase cognitive load and deplete the bandwidth required for high-signal preparation and disciplined pipeline pacing.

- Late-stage rejection -> elevated cognitive load and sunk-cost strain -> degraded preparation and pacing: Repeated near-miss outcomes after five-plus rounds consume time and attentional capacity, degrading performance in subsequent loops and turning each new cycle into a heavier tax on focus.

- Sustained rejection streak -> distorted probability estimation -> binary opportunity tunneling: Extrapolating current market selectivity and rejection streaks linearly across multi-year horizons produces extreme pessimism (such as assuming no recovery until 2035), narrowing perceived search options and stalling career execution.

The system exhibits instability at two coupling points: calibration drift, where interview rubrics ratchet upward without corresponding updates to role scope or compensation bands, and positive feedback in candidate perception, where repeated late-stage rejections compress perceived future states into extreme, rigid hypotheses. Left unchecked, these coupled dynamics turn a tough market into a self-reinforcing trap—driving engineers toward burnout, passive waiting for a 2021-style boom, or uncontested acceptance of compressed wage-to-skill terms. Breaking the cycle requires treating late-stage rejections as structural filter noise and shifting away from high-volume lottery loops toward deliberate, leverage-driven positioning.

From 2021 Euphoria to 2026 Scarcity: How the Bar Moved

For an experienced software engineer absorbing a string of late-stage interview rejections in 2026, the market can feel either broken or indicting. It is neither. The contraction between the 2021 hiring expansion and the constricted 2026 labor market is not a verdict on individual competence, nor is it a signal of terminal industry decline. Rather, it represents a coupled economic, organizational, and statistical filtering system—one engineered to extract Staff-level execution at Senior-level compensation. Under post-zero-interest-rate margin discipline, elevated capital costs and stricter return-on-invested-capital (ROIC) scrutiny have forced organizations to restructure headcount allocation. That capital constraint propagates systematically downward through leveling bands, interview rubric calibration, sequential funnel probability, and candidate feedback loops, turning hiring into an employer-side arbitrage mechanism.

Structural Comparison: 2021 Expansion vs. 2026 Contraction

Understanding why a candidate who cleared Staff+ loops in 2021 routinely stalls at the final round in 2026 requires comparing the operating rules of both regimes. The table below maps how capital availability reshapes every layer of the engineering hiring apparatus.

The structural takeaway is unambiguous: the benchmark itself has been re-indexed. What appears at the candidate level as sudden career friction is, at the institutional level, a deliberate shift from growth-at-any-cost capacity building to capital-constrained risk minimization.

Causal Mechanism Chains

These structural shifts do not occur in isolation; they operate as tightly coupled causal chains. Tracing how macroeconomic pressure translates into a Friday afternoon rejection email exposes why traditional, high-volume job-search tactics fail under current conditions.…

item.title: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.

An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”

Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

Among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”

The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip showed a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.

A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.

Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.

Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.

More baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.

What do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

Source: Wired | Published: 2026-11-20 23:24 UTC

Original link: https://www.wired.com/story/cops-are-being-extremely-corny-about-gta-vi/

item.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history

- Published

Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release, hitting $3.8bn (Â£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.

Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game.

To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (Â£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas.

Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch.

New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access.

In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast.

In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.

The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (Â£1.2bn) in just five days.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Research firm Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been on PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn (Â£3.44bn), adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.

GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.

The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.

The launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.

The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.

Police departments have also reminded Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement reached a fever pitch in the US.

NINLIVE

The Nine Inch Nails live archive

Explore shows, download recordings, stream audio, and follow the tape trail across every era. Fan run, not affiliated with the band.

From the archive

The Future Is Here - ninlive Streaming 1988-2026

Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.

I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.

Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

item.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

Carr: California rules “designed for a bygone era”

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

Source: Ars Technica | Published: 2026-11-20 22:28 UTC

item.title: One hand on the controller, one on the pizza roll: How America fed itself through GTA VI’s $3.79 billion launch night
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The biggest video game launch in years left millions of players with a practical problem: how to eat without putting down the controller.

Rockstar Games, a unit of Take-Two Interactive, said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales worldwide on its first day, which it called the biggest entertainment launch in history. With that demand, there are surely some tired people holding onto those controllers but hungry for a snack.

It seems like the delivery apps already planned for it. Uber Eats picked several of its Grand Theft Auto VI launch-day deals for food that could be eaten with one hand. In the U.S., the list included buy-one-get-one McNuggets at McDonald’s, boneless wings at Wingstop, pizza at Papa John’s and Whopper Jr. burgers at Burger King.

“We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game,” Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald said in a statement to Fortune.

Gamers ordered accordingly. Between midnight and 5 a.m. on launch night, Uber Eats orders in Miami, the real city behind the game’s Vice City, rose more than 30% from the prior two Thursdays, Macdonald said on X. Nationwide, orders of Red Bull Watermelon rose 95%, Totino’s Pizza Rolls 54% and Ghost Sour Strips 46%. Uber told Fortune it had no separate data on one-handed food orders.

DoorDash reported a similar pattern. Between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m. ET, orders for chips, burgers, fries and pizza each rose more than 10% compared with the average of the six prior Wednesdays, the company told Fortune. Energy drinks rose more than 20%. Miami led all major markets, with late-night orders up nearly 25%, and Philadelphia, Detroit and Atlanta also saw double-digit increases, according to DoorDash’s data dashboard. DoorDash said it could not compare the food increases with its overall order growth.

“A cultural moment”

Some of the biggest jumps were for gear, not food. Orders for controllers and gaming accessories rose 450% on DoorDash, HDMI cables 440% and headsets 70%. Searches for GTA VI on the app rose more than 940% in the week before launch.

“GTA 6 is more than a game launch. It’s a cultural moment that fans have been waiting years for,” Gina Igwe, DoorDash’s vice president of brand, creative and consumer marketing, said in a statement to Fortune.

Players who weren’t playing were watching. In its first two days, GTA VI drew more livestream watch time than any game has in its entire launch week, more than Elden Ring, Hogwarts Legacy and Cyberpunk 2077 drew in their first weeks combined, according to Streams Charts.

Total Twitch watch time rose 61% compared with the two days before launch, the firm said, while World of Warcraft and Counter-Strike lost about 31% of their Twitch watch time and Fortnite fell 60% on YouTube. Kick’s “Just Sleeping” category rose 176% as streamers ran round-the-clock GTA VI marathons.

Restaurant chains also moved to get a share. Popeyes is selling a Spice City sandwich, named after the game’s setting, through Nov. 22 and told players to order it through its app “between missions.” McDonald’s began taking delivery orders on Discord, the chat app many gamers use while they play. DoorDash ran offers with Wendy’s and the Cheesecake Factory, and Grubhub offered $10 off to its first 1,000 customers.

Analytics firm Sensor Tower expects the game to drive more than 50 million additional visits to U.S. food delivery and restaurant apps in its first 30 days, Reuters reported.

Neither company put a dollar figure on launch night. A rough Fortune estimate suggests the extra takeout spending was small next to the game itself. Uber and DoorDash together handled about $680 million in delivery orders a day worldwide in the third quarter, based on their earnings reports. If late-night hours make up roughly a tenth of that, and launch night lifted those orders 10% to 25%, the extra spending comes to roughly $7 million to $17 million. That’s about 1% to 2.5% of a normal day’s delivery business for the two companies, and less than half a percent of the $3.79 billion Rockstar says the game brought in on day one.

That shift fits what economists say about events like this one. Much of the money moves from one kind of spending to another rather than appearing from nowhere. “People just rearrange how they’re spending their free time,” Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, told Fortune before the launch.

Restaurants also had fewer hands. Missed restaurant shifts rose 92% week over week on Nov. 19, according to data from scheduling platform Harri shared with Fortune, covering 280,000 shifts. One in 14 shifts went unworked, compared with one in 27 the Thursday before, while sales at those restaurants fell less than 2%.

Grand Theft Auto VI came out Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, more than 13 years after its predecessor. Before the launch, a widely shared estimate claimed workers skipping their jobs to play would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion, a figure Matheson told Fortune he doesn’t believe. Office attendance barely moved. Wi-Fi logins at the more than 250 U.S. locations of Industrious, a coworking company owned by CBRE, fell about 5% on launch day compared with the previous three Thursdays, the company told Fortune.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 22:16 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/gta-grand-theft-auto-6-vi-food-delivery-services-orders/

item.title: BNP Paribas sees ‘panic selling’ as the AI selloff drags the S&P 500 into a correction and wipes out the Nasdaq’s 2026 gains
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The S&P 500 fell into a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back everything it had gained in 2026.

The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and the Dow also ended in correction territory. The S&P fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Investors were “panic selling” as they tried to judge whether enthusiasm for AI had peaked, Benedicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, told CNBC.

Anthropic led the AI slide, as Fortune reported Friday morning. The Claude maker raised $81.34 billion in an IPO that valued it at $1.414 trillion, and its shares fell about 9% Friday, their second day of trading, giving back much of Thursday’s 17% pop. Reuters cited worries about slower data-center expansion, higher borrowing costs and Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.

The people with the most money in stocks already felt it. Those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances in the University of Michigan’s November survey, which ran through Nov. 16, “consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets,” survey director Joanne Hsu said.

What the panic looked like

Chipmakers took the worst of it. Micron, hotlink]Broadcom[/hotlink], Nvidia, and AMD were down between roughly 12% and 14%. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, topped 30 for the first time since March, CNBC reported.

The selling wasn’t only in the U.S. Taiwan’s stock index fell 5.65% Friday, capping its steepest weekly drop since October 1997, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell about 5%.

Washington added to it. President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build data centers abroad, CNBC reported.

At midday, some analysts still saw a rotation.

“Money is leaving tech, not the market,” independent tech analyst Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter, wrote in a note at 12:59 p.m. He said the Dow and the equal-weight S&P were higher at the time. His advice: Avoid AI stocks “while they’re being combative teenagers.” He also pointed to credit: SpaceX had to raise the yield on its $32 billion debt sale to 8.3%, which he read as the “capital spigot” closing for weaker AI borrowers such as CoreWeave and Nebius.

The calm-down chorus

Most of the Street said the drop would pass.

“Given the solid economic and fundamental backdrop, the move appears to be highly sentiment driven,” Chris Larkin, head of trading at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley, said in commentary sent to Fortune. He added that “only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983” turned into bear markets.

Deutsche Bank’s Binky Chadha called the market “very oversold” and said growth and earnings remained strong, according to CNBC. JPMorgan Asset Management chief global strategist David Kelly told Seeking Alpha markets were overdue for a tech correction. Chuck Carlson, CEO of Horizon Investment Services, told Reuters the market may be in a correction within a bull market.

E*Trade’s own research is less soothing. A March 2025 E*TRADE study of the 14 times since 1983 that the S&P 500 first closed 10% or more below a record found five became bear markets. But the index fell another 10% or more after closing in correction six of those 14 times, and in 1990 and 1998 it came within a point of bear territory. The median total drop from the record was 19.9%.

The backdrop Larkin calls solid includes a rate hike on the way. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday the central bank will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high, Reuters reported. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, per CME FedWatch, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.

The Fed meets Dec. 9. Investors will find out then whether Friday was panic or just early.

Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of this article. The reporter independently reported and verified the factual claims in this article, and a human editor reviewed it before publication.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 21:38 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/sp-500-correction-panic-selling-ai-selloff-nasdaq-2026-gains-bnp-paribas/

item.title: Fed governor admits people now think higher inflation is the new normal. ‘That’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Fed Governor Chris Waller says Americans are starting to treat 3% inflation as normal, and he thinks the central bank may need to “shock people” out of it.

The latest consumer price index also showed inflation is heating up more than expected, drifting further away from the Fed’s 2% target. And given that it’s been above that threshold for more than five years, it’s getting harder for consumers and businesses to see higher prices as a temporary blip.

In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Waller warned that inflation is spreading beyond the areas most affected by higher energy prices or tariffs, including into so-called core services. He recalled talking to someone last week who said his business passed on a 3% price hike to consumers because that’s what he thinks his customers can swallow.

“And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down,” Waller explained. “So you might need to, like, shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute, 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward.’”

Once households and businesses expect prices to keep rising 3% a year, they set wages and prices to match, the kind of spiral the Fed worries about after more than five years above its 2% target.

Maintaining consumers’ inflation expectations is a top priority for the Fed. It previously held off on a more hawkish stance, saying expectations were still well anchored. But in Waller’s view, that’s no longer the case.

“People are starting to think 3% may be the norm. And if you’re a firm, and the consumer’s resilient and seems to be spending, why not pass through three,” Waller warned. “And that’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking, is that it’s not going to be three, and we have to do something to try to bring it back down. We can’t wait. We can’t do this in, like, the next two years.”

Because people are starting to become more accepting of higher prices, he thinks the central bank needs to be “a little more aggressive” with rate hikes, including a potential jumbo-size half-point increase at the Fed’s Dec. 8–9 meetings.

A half-point move would lift the Fed’s benchmark rate to a range of 4.25% to 4.5%, from 3.75% to 4% now. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years, then held steady in October.

Wall Street isn’t there yet. Futures are fully pricing in a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Waller said a quarter-point could do the job if the Fed clearly signaled another hike in January. But Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on the grounds that it ties policymakers’ hands.

The problem has been complicated by the fact that the effects of President Donald Trump’s tariffs have been dragged out instead of hitting all at once, as negotiations and legal challenges kept the levies on again and off again. Meanwhile, businesses didn’t pass on the full cost of tariffs at once but spread it out.

At the same time, the Iran war doesn’t seem to be winding down anytime soon as Trump has shot down further talks. Although oil prices have come down from highs, they are still volatile and spike whenever fighting in the Persian Gulf heats up again. The cumulative effect is weighing on attitudes.

Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, released the same day as Waller’s interview, back up his worry: Fed staff flagged the risk that longer-run inflation expectations could have become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation.

On Friday, Fed Governor Lisa Cook echoed Waller’s concerns about consumer psychology as she explained her dissenting vote to hike rates at the last meeting.

“My vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation,” which “has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward,” she said, according to the text of a speech to be presented at a conference in Chile.

Still, other policymakers signaled more caution. New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday that there’s no need for “dramatic action,” arguing that the more gradual approach in recent months is working well.

He added that the economy remains resilient and the labor market is solid, even as he acknowledged that inflation isn’t moving in the right direction. But that resilience is also what’s allowing businesses to pass on bigger price hikes.

As a result, one big hike may not be the end of it. Waller said the Fed needs to reverse the three rate cuts it made in 2025, and may have to go further.

“If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn’t bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn’t going to bring it down,” he told CNBC. “So we may have to go above … three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down.”

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 21:08 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/fed-rate-hikes-higher-inflation-expectations-unanchored-chris-waller/

item.title: Here’s who’s getting the richest from Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the company’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich.

Dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes. These commitments, though, are voluntary and not legally binding, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing.

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic announced that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion.

After pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the company opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat, the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart.

The record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the most.

Billionaire founders

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic’s president and chair of the board, Daniela Amodei, are among the figures most commonly associated with the company. But there are another five cofounders who are cashing in as well.

Each of its seven cofounders owns between 237 million and 241 million shares after the offering. At the stock’s price of about $85 on Friday, that means each founder has holdings worth approximately $20 billion, putting them (at least on paper) in the same league as Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who has a net worth of $21 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Each founder also sold approximately 3.38 million shares in the IPO, worth about $280 million at the offering price.

Despite owning a minority of the company’s equity, Anthropic’s cofounders control 50.1% of its shareholder voting power. The nearly equal distribution of shares among the seven founders is unusual for a Silicon Valley startup, Fortune reported.

Venture capital winners

Besides its cofounders, some Silicon Valley investors are also set to win big. Lightspeed Venture Partners, an early backer of Snapchat, led a $3.5 billion funding round in Anthropic in March 2025 when the company was valued at $61.5 billion. The VC firm owns less than 2% of the company, according to Bloomberg, yet its stake is still reportedly worth tens of billions of dollars.

Other VCs like Menlo Ventures also own a stake representing less than 2% of the company, Bloomberg reported. Iconiq has invested more than $6 billion in Anthropic since 2025, and its stake is worth more than $26 billion, the outlet reported. Anthropic in total has more than 400 venture investors, according to PitchBook, yet no VC firm owns more than 5%, Fortune reported.

The company’s historic IPO means even some smaller stakes are now worth billions. Sound Ventures, the venture firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher, invested about $435 million in Anthropic and owns about 0.5% of the company, Bloomberg reported. It’s unclear, though, how much Kutcher himself benefited from the trade as the actor best known for his role on That ’70s Show stepped down as general partner at the firm earlier this year.

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also owns about 1% of Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, putting his stake’s value at about $11 billion at Friday’s share price.

One early investor who won’t be reaping the rewards is FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is serving a sentence of 25 years in prison after being convicted on fraud and conspiracy charges. Bankman-Fried has appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court. The trading firm he founded, Alameda Research, invested $500 million in Anthropic, but FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold most of its stake in 2024 to repay creditors. Among the buyers was Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street, which stands to reap a multibillion-dollar windfall.

Employee millionaires

Many of the company’s roughly 5,300 employees are also getting rich thanks to generous stock-based compensation. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimated that 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity in the company at a $1.35 trillion valuation, Reuters reported.

Some of the earliest employees stand to benefit disproportionately. At least 400 early hires could hold equity worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

To be sure, it’s hard to estimate which employees hold how much stock because Anthropic’s IPO filing discloses aggregate equity awards but not their distribution among individual employees.

Now that Anthropic is public, non-founder employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of certain holdings, and up to another 35% following the release of Anthropic’s 2026 financial results.

Big Tech gains

Some of the biggest gains from the company’s IPO will go to two Big Tech giants, Amazon and Google. Anthropic’s IPO filing estimated that Amazon would own 14.6% of the company’s outstanding shares and Google would own 13.4%.

Amazon’s stake stems from billions of dollars in investments the company has made in Anthropic dating back to 2023, around the time it had just 160 employees. At the time, Amazon committed an initial $1.25 billion as part of a deal to ultimately invest $4 billion in Anthropic. In exchange Anthropic agreed to make Amazon Web Services its primary cloud provider for critical workloads and make Claude available to AWS customers.

In total, Amazon invested $8 billion in convertible notes between 2023 and 2025 and put in another $10 billion in preferred stock in 2026.

Google has also poured billions into Anthropic, including $10 billion it invested in a financing round earlier this year and another $10 billion in a private placement alongside the IPO.

At the company’s roughly $85 per share stock price Friday, Amazon’s 1.94 billion shares would be worth about $165 billion, while Google’s 1.77 billion shares would be worth around $151 billion.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 20:42 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/heres-whos-getting-the-richest-from-anthropics-81-billion-ipo-tech-stocks-ai-dario-amodei-daniela-amodei/

item.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

- Published

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain Â£5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or Â£17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-20 16:41 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm1wr029evnqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Alabama Power Announces $160 Million Rate Decrease for 2027 After Pushback on High Energy Costs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Alabama Power announced Friday its electric rates would decrease across the board next year, saving its 1.5 million customers approximately $160 million on their energy bills.

The company attributed the savings to projected increases in revenue from large data center contracts next year.

“In January, our customers will see their rates go down because of the growth we’re seeing across the state,” Alabama Power CEO Jeff Peoples said in a news release. “Alabama is growing and we’re making sure that growth works for all of our customers.”

The company news release said that a home or business using 1,000 kilowatt-hours each month would save more than $50 a year, compared to current rates.

Electricity costs have been a major political issue in Alabama for the past year, after an Inside Climate News investigation last November showed Alabama Power customers paid the highest total electric bills in the country in 2024, driven by its above-average rates and Alabama’s very high electricity usage.

In filings made Friday with the Alabama Public Service Commission, the company announced a projected 2027 income of $1.76 billion, higher than its currently allowed rate of return set by the PSC.

Unlike most regulated utilities in the United States, Alabama Power operates under a formula-based rate mechanism called the Rate Stabilization and Equalization factor, created by the PSC in 1982.

Under that system, rates are adjusted up or down automatically every January based on the company’s projections for the upcoming year, without the formal rate case hearings that most other states use to set electricity rates.

Those projections for 2027 triggered the changes, which will take effect in January.

Alabama Power also said it will comply with the commission’s request to stop billing customers for part of its advertising budget beginning in 2027. That change is expected to save the average customer about four cents per month, the company said.

Critics Say Tax Cut, Not Data Centers, Drive Decrease

Daniel Tait, executive director of clean energy advocacy group Energy Alabama, said the company should not get credit for lowering rates when the formula dictated the decrease.

“Alabama Power customers should not be fooled,” Tait said in an email. “The utility wants a public parade for handing back money it was on track to overcharge customers.”

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Tait also said the company is crediting data centers for the decrease, but does not mention that a massive cut in the company’s tax bill generated even more savings.

“The company credits data centers, but its own numbers show there would be no cut without a roughly $180 million drop in its tax bill, which the company ties to nuclear tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act,” Tait said. “Even after this action, the company’s own filing shows its return on equity, a marker for its profits, remaining above the national average.”

Relief for Customers Paying Country’s Highest Bills

Two weeks after the ICN investigation was published last November, U.S. Sen. Katie Britt said Alabama had the “highest rates in the Southeast,” amid a debate about a hyperscale data center project currently under construction in Bessemer, just west of Birmingham.

In December, the PSC approved a two-year rate freeze proposed by Alabama Power, delaying scheduled increases surrounding the purchase of a gas-fired power plant, and blocking rate increases until 2028.

Then in the spring, fierce public backlash against high electricity prices spurred state lawmakers to pass sweeping utility legislation that will dramatically reshape the PSC, but will not require the formal rate case hearings that most other states use.

The bill will expand the PSC from three members to seven next year, and create a governor-appointed secretary of energy who will set the PSC’s agenda and “have authority over personnel and administrative functions of the commission.”

The secretary can only be overruled by a vote of five of the seven commissioners.

The two incumbent PSC commissioners on the ballot this year were defeated in GOP primaries, leaving PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond as the lone returning member next year.

Britt issued a news release Friday, taking credit for next year’s decrease.

“I asked Alabama Power to find a way to lower rates—not just freeze them, but achieve lower power bills for Alabama households,” Britt said in the release. “Today, I am excited to say that is happening.

“I am proud to have successfully led this charge and that it’s resulted in putting more money back in hardworking Alabamians’ pockets.”

Tait, from Energy Alabama, said the bigger issue is the high rate of return that Alabama Power earns. The company reported $1.52 billion in profit through the first three quarters of 2026.

“Alabamians want real relief on their electric bills, and that comes from a cut to what Alabama Power is allowed to profit,” he said. “Sure, people will take the $4 per month but shuffling tax credits around doesn’t cut it.”

item.title: Court Delays Plan to Detonate Toxic Explosives in Iowa
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Plans to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at an Eastern Iowa ammunition plant are on hold after the Army postponed the operation and a federal appeals court temporarily halted an emergency permit from the Environmental Protection Agency.

Initially scheduled for Friday, the planned explosion generated immense public outcry and concern from public health experts, environmentalists and elected officials who say residents received inadequate notice and guidance regarding the impacts of lead dust on their health and the environment.

Lead azide is a common primary explosive in bombs. After decades in storage at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, 68 barrels of the compound have become dangerously unstable and require emergency disposal.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced late Thursday that the detonation would be rescheduled to Monday. But hours later, a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit placed an administrative stay on the EPA’s detonation permit, indefinitely delaying the operation.

The ruling came less than 24 hours after environmental law organization Earthjustice, representing the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, sued the EPA over its permit and filed an emergency motion asking the court to suspend it.

In their suit, the petitioners argued that the decision-making process lacked transparency and that the Army failed to adequately explore alternatives to detonation. “Within the permit, we just do not see enough things that will protect human health and the environment,” said Thien Chau, a senior attorney for Earthjustice. He described the planned detonation as “abnormal and extraordinary.”

The court could rule on the emergency motion at any point in the next few days, Chau said.

A Ticking Time Bomb

During a March safety review at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, officials discovered that stored lead azide had dissolved and reformed into irregularly shaped, highly volatile crystals. Friction, heat or shock could easily trigger spontaneous detonation.

Rather than risk an accidental explosion by leaving the barrels in storage, relocating them or chemically neutralizing the contents, all alternatives the Army considered, the department opted to conduct a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide, according to its environmental assessment. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit for the detonation last Friday, citing an “unacceptable” risk of accidental combustion.

Even with mitigation technology like blast containment barriers and water misters in place, the explosion will generate a lead-containing dust cloud that could deposit the neurotoxin across hundreds of miles in an area where tens of thousands of Iowans live.

Residents of Middletown were informed of the planned detonation at a town hall in October. But state officials and most Iowans learned about the explosion just days before it was scheduled to take place.

Maps released by the Army in a public advisory early this week projected surface deposition of lead 50 miles northwest of Middletown, with airborne exposure as far as 100 miles afield.

A spokesperson for Gov. Kim Reynolds said that the advisory was the first she had heard of the operation.

The projected ranges for the dust cloud shrank significantly in updated maps released Wednesday, which the Army says reflect changing weather forecasts. Their most recent projections showed toxic lead dust settling on surfaces over a smaller region that extends at least 30 miles north of the plant and up to 10 miles wide.

Planning for Toxic Debris

The Army’s projections suggest outdoor lead dust levels in the plume’s path could exceed federal benchmarks for indoor lead levels in homes and childcare facilities, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa.

Still, the precise amount and location of lead that would be released by the blast is unknown and depends on weather conditions and the effectiveness of the Army’s engineered controls, O’Shaughnessy said.

According to the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency, the Army is required to use high-end estimates to avoid underestimating the potential impact of the detonation. The Army did not respond to questions about more specific ranges of lead concentrations.

Leading up to the planned Friday detonation, the Army advised residents to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and set heating and cooling systems to “recirculate” for a few hours after the planned blast. The Army also advised residents to clean their cars and hose down play surfaces and windowsills once the cloud settled.

Any surfaces typically touched by children would be especially important to clean, said O’Shaughnessy. As a neurotoxin, lead is most harmful to small children and infants with developing brains and nervous systems.

The EPA emergency permit requires the Army to conduct monitoring before, during and after detonation. In addition, researchers at the University of Iowa scrambled to set up independent air and soil monitoring following the Army’s announcement early this week, said David Cwiertny, director of the university’s Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Many residents of the heavily agricultural state have expressed concern about the lingering effects of lead dust for soil, crops and livestock, Cwiertny said. Scientists will rely on field samples taken after the explosion to gauge the impact on agriculture and animals.

“We know that unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil, because those surfaces are hard to clean,” he said.

The Army has not issued specific guidance for livestock producers in the exposure zone. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended livestock be kept at an alternate location or indoors until the air plume could pass.

The department also suggested that producers ask the U.S. Army to collect soil and forage samples at their farms after the detonation, power wash the exteriors of buildings and equipment and work with a veterinarian to monitor livestock for signs of lead poisoning.

Leaders Call For Clarity

On Thursday night, Gov. Reynolds issued a statement saying she had spoken to Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle and asked that he delay the detonation. Governor-elect Rob Sand and U.S. Senator-elect Josh Turek also called on military leadership to postpone the operation until Iowans could be given more information about the decision-making process.

In light of growing public interest in the detonation, the Department of the Army, Department of Health and Human Services and Environmental Protection Agency issued a joint statement Friday morning.

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement read.
