item.title: US leases American Samoan seabed for mining in auction deemed illegal by court
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- On Nov. 19, the U.S. government auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of American Samoan seabed for $6 million, despite a federal court ruling that found the lease sale to be illegal for not taking into account impacts on endangered species.

- The lease sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals.

- Critics warn that seabed mining in the waters of American Samoa could harm the marine environment and threaten the cultural, food security and economic interests of local communities.

- A pending legal challenge could invalidate the auction and any leases issued.

The U.S. government has auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of the American Samoan seabed, despite public opposition and a federal court ruling that found the sale to be illegal. The sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals.

The auction, which took place on the morning of Nov. 19 in Thousand Oaks, California, was publicly livestreamed, offering two vast lots of American Samoan seabed: One covering about 15 million acres, and the other about 16 million acres. Mongabay attended the livestream.

Just two bidders showed up: A U.S. company called Wetstone U.S. Ventures and the Norwegian company Adepth. However, only Wetstone participated in the bidding process. By the end of the auction, which lasted approximately 20 minutes, Wetstone had secured both leases at the starting price of $3 million each, equivalent to approximately 19 U.S. cents per acre.

In 2024, American Samoa, a U.S. territory, imposed a moratorium on deep-sea mining in waters extending up to 3 nautical miles from its coastline. The U.S. government has jurisdiction over the remainder of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), which extends 200 nautical miles from shore, allowing it to pursue seabed mineral activities in this area without approval from the American Samoan government.

In a statement released on Nov. 16, a few days before the auction took place, Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, the governor of American Samoa, called the lease sale an “historic moment” for his nation.

“For more than 3,000 years, our Polynesian ancestors explored and navigated the vast Pacific Ocean,” Pula said. “Today, we stand at the threshold of a new era of exploration, one that could unlock scientific knowledge, create economic opportunities, and strengthen American Samoa’s role in America’s strategic future in the Pacific.”

Critics say that any mining activities in this area would harm the marine environment, particularly the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a 34,964-square kilometer (13,500-square mile) protected reef ecosystem adjacent to the lease areas that supports a range of endangered and threatened species, including sea turtles, sharks and cetaceans. Members of the American Samoan community and their allies also argue that deep-sea mining would disregard the cultural, food security and economic importance of their waters.

The Marine Minerals Administration (MMA), a federal agency within the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI), says it will responsibly pursue deep-sea mining in American Samoan waters, and that this activity is necessary to secure minerals critical for U.S. national security. Proponents of the industry argue that deep-sea minerals are needed for producing fighter jets, weaponry and renewable energy technologies.

The U.S. push to begin mining the deep sea follows U.S. President Donald Trump administration’s release in April 2025 of an executive order calling for the accelerated development of the industry. In addition to pursuing deep-sea mining in federal waters, the U.S. is also looking to mine in international waters, including in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific Ocean and the South Pacific Ocean.

Forty-five nations have called for a moratorium or precautionary pause on the industry due to a number of concerns, including the potential destruction of the marine environment and a lack of research on the impacts of the fledgling industry. Deep-sea mining has not yet begun on a commercial scale anywhere in the world.

Speaking just before the auction of the American Samoan seabed began, MMA Acting Director Michael Olsen said the lease sale was “another step in securing American self-reliance while honoring our responsibility to care for the waters and resources we’ll pass on to the next generation.”

“As we look to America’s next 250 years, we want future generations to inherit a nation that can build and innovate here at home, on the lands and in the waters that we’ve stewarded,” Olsen said.

Douglas Boren, who leads the MMA’s Pacific office, emphasized before the auction that the leases would only permit preliminary seabed surveys and data collection, and that any subsequent testing or commercial extraction would require further DOI approval and environmental review.

The lease sale proceeded despite a federal court in Hawaiʻi ruling on Nov. 16 in favor of community and conservation groups that had sued the National Marine Fisheries Service, an agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, for violating the nation’s Endangered Species Act by greenlighting the deep-sea mining lease sale.

Chris Eaton, a senior attorney at the U.S. nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, called the DOI’s decision to proceed with the lease sale “lawless.”

“I thought it was pretty remarkable that in the live auction, they didn’t even acknowledge that ruling,” Eaton told Mongabay. “They’re ignoring that a federal court said what they’re doing is illegal, and they’re proceeding as if everything is just fine.”

“I am not sure why they decided to go forward,” he added. “I think it was kind of a shock.”

Eaton said Earthjustice has a second motion pending against the MMA that challenges the agency’s legal authority to proceed with the sale. If successful, the motion could invalidate the auction process and any leases issued.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau Foundation, an environmental organization in American Samoa that opposes deep-sea mining, said she was “filled with frustration.” On Nov. 19, Suluai-Mahuka and other environmental advocates took part in a protest outside the site of the auction in Thousand Oaks.

“It’s very mind-boggling to think that they can put a price tag on our home and our waters, as if the impacts are not going to be felt by the real people who live in the ocean,” Suluai-Mahuka told Mongabay. “But this also sets a blueprint for future lease sales like CNMI [Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands] and Guam and Alaska and Virginia.”

The next planned lease sale, for 27 million hectares (67 million acres) of seabed in the CNMI, is scheduled for Dec. 16.

“While we’re extremely disappointed, we’re actually not surprised with how aggressive this timeline has been in this process,” Suluai-Mahuka said. “But this is not the end of our fight. We are going to continue to fight with every single bit of our being to protect our home and our children’s futures.”

Banner image: A helmet jellyfish (Periphylla periphylla) descending to the seafloor. Image by ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

Elizabeth Claire Alberts is a senior staff writer for Mongabay and was a 2024-2025 fellow with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network. Find her on Bluesky and LinkedIn.

Experts say ‘bare bones’ US laws are unfit to regulate nascent deep-sea mining industry

US prepares to auction leases for seabed mining blocks in federal waters

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 22:18 UTC

Original link: https://news.mongabay.com/2026/11/us-leases-american-samoan-seabed-for-mining-in-auction-deemed-illegal-by-court/

item.title: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.

The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.

On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.

Several Cop insiders said Saudi Arabia was one of the countries playing an obstructive role. The petrostate has gained a reputation over the decades for using the Cop process to slow action. Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in the final agreement as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at the advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there”. He said: “It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests.”

Eight countries called for reference to “a clear transition away from fossil fuels” to be restored into the text of any agreement. Panama, Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, the Solomon Islands and Sweden outlined vital issues they said must be addressed, including ensuring polluting countries paid into funds for developing countries to adapt to the climate crisis.

Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, said: “It is not acceptable to have a Cop or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly.”

Panama had sent an open letter to the president of the negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, with a list of demands the country said were not negotiable.

“Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work,” said Bowen. On Friday afternoon, he said: “There is still a spirit of making it work. People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, let’s give up and go home.”

In a dramatic press conference on Friday morning, African ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone said African people were being asked to pay for a crisis they did not cause. They accused rich countries of simultaneously attempting a third exploitation of the continent – after slavery and colonialism – by using carbon taxes to prevent Africans from making use of their wealth of critical minerals to industrialise.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who was ministerial chair of the African group of negotiators, said: “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them. We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries, that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

A vital request of African nations was for discussion of climate finance. All week civil society observers have accused richer countries, led by the EU, of obstructing progress in talks on money.

The chief climate negotiator for Europe said on Friday that it was already the world leading climate finance donor. A senior EU official said: “We, together with the EU member states, are providing €32.3bn [£27bn] from public sources and mobilising €9.3bn in private finance in 2025 to support developing countries. We’re doing by far the most.”

The last Cop meeting to finish on time was in Italy in 2003. Some talks have dragged into the Sunday after the scheduled Friday finish.

Source: The Guardian Environment | Published: 2026-11-20 20:04 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/20/cop31-talks-overtime-fossil-fuels-vanish-from-draft-deal

item.title: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium. The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden.

The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation.

Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.”

The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement.

Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care in the same way gorillas and elephants do.”

Along with spiders, scorpions, crabs and other animals with jointed exoskeletons insects are part of the taxonomic group Arthropoda.

A highlight of the insect-based zoo is a leaf-cutter ant (Atta cephalotes) colony from a rainforest in Trinidad. It shows the complex society of ants that farm fungus, their food, on leaves that they forage.

“The different chambers the ants live in are made out of blown glass, so guests have the opportunity to see how the entire ant colony operates and works cooperatively,” Miller said.

The BUGarium also exhibits insects and spiders from New Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert.

“Connecting our guests to nature is a cornerstone of what we do at the BioPark, and at the BUGarium our focus is creating meaningful connections between guests and arthropods,” Miller said.

Other U.S. zoos like the San Diego Zoo and Cincinnati Zoo also have dedicated exhibits for connecting people with insects. However, insect and spider exhibits are not nearly as common as exhibits of popular vertebrate species.

“The BUGarium is part of a small group of facilities dedicated to live insects and arthropods in the United States. Our numbers may be small, but like the animals in our care, can have a huge impact,” Miller said. “We are proud to be a part of the story of connecting people to arthropods and promoting their conservation.”

Banner image: Leaf-cutter ants at ABQ BioPark BUGarium.

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 19:59 UTC

Original link: https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2026/11/renovated-bugarium-in-the-us-aims-to-connect-people-and-insects/

item.title: Trump Administration Awards First-Ever Deep-Sea Mining Exploration Leases
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

In a historic first, the Department of Interior has leased more than 31 million acres of Pacific waters to a deep-sea mining company seeking to exploit mineral-rich deposits from the ocean floor off American Samoa.

“This is the first time that a lease has been issued for deep-sea mining in U.S. waters,” said Arlo Hemphill, U.S. project lead against deep-sea mining for Greenpeace USA.

Deep-sea mining is a highly contested, emerging industry that aims to extract rock-like deposits on the seabed called polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years. They contain cobalt, copper, manganese and nickel—so-called “critical minerals” used in batteries, electronics and other devices that have historically been mined on land. To date, no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere in the world.

Scientists, environmentalists and Indigenous peoples with strong cultural connections to the ocean aim to stop the industry from moving forward at all.

“Once mining strips away habitat that took millions of years to form, no amount of money can bring it back,” said Hemphill in a statement. “Congress should press the administration to suspend these leases before work begins.”

The lease sale took place Thursday, during a live auction held at the Ventura County Fire Department in Thousand Oaks, California, as Hemphill and dozens of other activists from American Samoa and across the Pacific rallied, prayed and sang outside in protest.

“This is not just seabed on a map. This is our home, our livelihoods, our identity, and our responsibility to protect,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, American Samoa’s youth and environment nonprofit, who traveled from American Samoa to protest the auction. “Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale,” she said in a statement.

Representatives from just two companies attended the auction, including Adepth Minerals Inc., from Norway, and Wetstone U.S. Ventures, a New York-based offshore critical minerals exploration and deep-sea mining company.

Ultimately, Wetstone bid $6 million on two areas marked for mineral exploration that lie adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a marine protected area established by President George W. Bush in 2009 to protect more than 10,000 square miles of ocean from commercial fishing and other forms of extraction.

The bid made Wetstone the provisional winner of the auction, according to a spokesperson from the Marine Minerals Administration. The new office was established earlier this year within the Department of Interior to help promote the Trump administration’s agenda to secure critical minerals.

“A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, in a statement about Thursday’s auction. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

The areas offered for leasing will be open for exploration activities, which include mapping and surveying the seabed to locate mineral rich deposits. Actual mining would require further federal approvals. But Hemphill and others warn that exploration in itself is a dangerous step towards paving the way for an industry that could threaten ocean ecosystems and the people that depend on them.

“The industry will push to move from surveys to exploration to extraction, putting profits ahead of marine life and trampling the culture, livelihood and objections of communities that have said no again and again,” Hemphill said.

Ever since the proposed lease sale was announced earlier this year, many American Samoan leaders and communities have voiced their concerns. Several lawsuits were filed against the Trump Administration to stop it from happening.

Just a few days before the lease sale, a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled the Marine Minerals Administration had violated the Endangered Species Act by approving the lease sale without taking into account the potential impacts of exploration and mining on endangered species.

The areas leased are home to several dozen endangered species including the blue whale, fin whale, sei whale and sperm whale, as well as the leatherback sea turtle, oceanic whitetip shark and giant manta ray.

Many of these species are already threatened by climate change, which is altering their sources of prey and migration patterns. More than 1000 marine science and policy experts from 75 countries say deep-sea mining could further add to the stress these marine animals are facing.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” said Chris Eaton, attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that represented American Samoan and Hawaiian plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” he said in a statement Thursday.

About This Story

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. item.title: I Tested 6 Popular Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies to Find the Best One for Thanksgiving Dinner
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

I Tested 6 Popular Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies to Find the Best One for Thanksgiving Dinner

Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

6. Aldi

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

5. Walmart

Selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

4. Trader Joe’s

The pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

This pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

Bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

3. Marie Callender’s

Marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

In terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

2. Kroger

At almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

1. Albertson’s

The pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

Which store-bought pie is your fave? Let us know in the comments below!

Source: Taste of Home | Published: 2026-11-20 23:40 UTC

item.title: Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls

What you’ll need

- 9" Round Cake Pan $21 $16 At Amazon

- Stand Mixer $400 $280 At Amazon

- Scale $26 At Amazon

- French Rolling Pin $21 At Amazon

- Set of 6 Pastry Rulers $20 At Kitchen Jukebox

Recipe information

- Total Time 3½ hours

- Yield Makes 12 rolls (8–12 servings)

Ingredients

DOUGH

2¼

5¾

1

1

⅓

1

½

FILLING

½

1

2

2

½

FROSTING AND ASSEMBLY

4

8

1¼

1

1

¼

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- DOUGH Step 1 Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool. Step 2 Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again. Step 3 Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

- FILLING Step 4 While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

- FROSTING AND ASSEMBLY Step 5 Butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer. Step 6 Starting at edge closest to you, tightly roll up dough into a log; roll log seam side down. Using a sharp serrated knife and long sawing motions, trim ends of log; discard. Using serrated knife or, preferably, unflavored dental floss, cut log in half crosswise, then cut each half into 6 equal rounds. (If using dental floss, slide floss underneath dough, then cross over top and pull ends through.) Nestle 6 rounds, cut side down, in each prepared cake pan. Cover with damp kitchen towels and let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, about 30–50 minutes. Step 7 Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes. Step 8 Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable. Step 9 Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

item.title: This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

And while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Venison

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

Wildfowl

Roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn Porridge and Bread

Corn was one of the most important foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively new to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

One traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

Fish and Shellfish

The waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

The English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

Squash and Pumpkin

Squash and pumpkin were important crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

The English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in New England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

Beans and Stews

The Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous New England roots that remains an American favorite.

Wild Fruits and Nuts

The forests and wetlands of New England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

Nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

Source: Taste of Home | Published: 2026-11-20 22:33 UTC

item.title: This Egg Wash Secret Makes the Prettiest Pie Crusts Every Time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

This Egg Wash Secret Makes the Prettiest Pie Crusts Every Time

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

What is the egg wash trick?

Paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

Beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

The difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

What does salt do to an egg wash?

If you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

The egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

item.title: The Secret to the Creamiest Mac and Cheese Comes in a Can
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The Secret to the Creamiest Mac and Cheese Comes in a Can

Making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

Which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

Why does evaporated milk make the creamiest mac and cheese?

Evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

More importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

How to Use Evaporated Milk in Mac and Cheese

One of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

The same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a big pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC

Twenty artists and designers across the Americas will be featured in "Malvestir" at MoMA PS1 this spring, probing the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

The exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach new, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways."

"Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary."

Source: Hyperallergic | Published: 2026-11-20 22:58 UTC

item.title: In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

An intergenerational group of artists confronts technology as both a pathogen and a cure for today’s cultural ailments in the husk of an office at 260 Madison.

A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

“We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”

Rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a new immersive Japanese hentai company through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

Both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a new work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion.

Having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators said they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols.

“He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva said regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very important work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”

Meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the New Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

Yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

“My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.…
