item.title: Todas sostenemos una llama contra el viento
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Traducción: Majel Reyes Quesada

No considero un insulto que me confundan con una prostituta. Ellas se levantan y se van a trabajar. Es más de lo que puedo decir de mí algunos días.

Esa vez, no fue la primera ni la última. Los faroles iluminaban los adoquines de Sevilla. Yo andaba por la catedral que resguarda los restos de Cristóbal Colón junto a las riquezas saqueadas al llamado Nuevo Mundo.

Dos generaciones atrás, mis ancestros se marcharon de España a Cuba y, poco después, abandonaron la isla y se fueron a los Estados Unidos. Somos la diáspora, océanos de distancia entre nuestro linaje. Pero esa noche de 2014, apenas me encontraba a una cuadra de mi esposo y de mi bebé, ambos dormidos. Mi abuela sureña habría dicho que me había ido de juerga —mi primer trago en solitario desde que di a luz. Una libertad impensable.

Llevaba los labios pintados, pero mi vestido no era ajustado. Hecho que no debería importarte a la hora de juzgar, pero te importa. De regreso al hotel, me crucé con un hombre de piernas arqueadas que le dijo a la señora que colgaba de su brazo: “Ya ves cómo se pone esta calle por las noches”. La presencia de dos mujeres sin acompañantes en la misma calle (yo no era la única) confundía al hombre, que asumió que éramos prostitutas. “Sí”, asintió su mujer.

No sé lo que la otra dama pudo haber pensado de mí mientras fumaba su cigarrillo tras las cuerdas aterciopeladas de la recepción. Tenía una mirada cómplice, un brillo si se quiere, pero ¿acaso no la tenemos todos? ¿Cómo evitarlo? Siglos de civilización no han corregido la creencia de que toda mujer tiene precio. Basta con afilar cada mirada en arma.

Consideremos otra ocasión en la ciudad de Brujas. En el verano de 2012, después de graduarme de la Maestría en Bellas Artes, hice un recorrido por Europa del Norte. Sí, soy privilegiada. Allí me senté en un café de una gran plaza. Más adelante, los canales zumbaban con los barcos de turistas, el eco del bullicio resonaba en una basílica donde cuentan que se conserva un trozo de tela empapado en sangre, una reliquia de Jesús, quien reconocía a las prostitutas como mujeres dignas de respeto. Pocos hombres pueden resistirse a un ritual de limpieza, y también estaba aquello de usar el propio pelo para secarle los pies.

Del otro lado del café, habían juntado dos mesas para un grupo de hombres que debatían sobre fútbol. Empezaron a hablar sobre mí en francés. No te voy a aburrir con sus muchos comentarios sobre mi belleza. Cuando uno se levantó para sacarme conversación, su amigo lo cogió del brazo y le previno: Arrête ça. Tu la vois, toute seule avec un livre. C’est une putain. El otro hombre se burló, pero sus acompañantes deliberaron y confirmaron que seguramente era así.

A lo mejor, fue el libro de Lolita. Estudié Nabokov por su narrador antipático disfrazado en prosa de terciopelo. Leía y escribía todas las mañanas en algún café, interpretando la vida que siempre quise. Excepto que mientras yo proyectaba Escritora, ellos veían Puta.

Al día siguiente me fui a Ámsterdam y frecuenté cafeterías del Barrio Rojo. Frente a la entrada de un burdel pasé por delante de un portero moreno. “Te quiero apoyar”, me dijo. No me percaté del significado de sus palabras hasta que giré por el puente donde planeaba tomar una foto. Una bandada de cisnes se deslizaba por el canal. Las aguas oscuras danzaban con los neones y sus reflejos de las mujeres tras el cristal. Quería quedarme con aquella imagen para cuando fuese mayor y menos libre. En cambio, recuerdo asimilar la frase gradualmente —como si la escuchase despacio— a medida que su significado se colaba en mi ensueño. El hombre pensó que yo trabajaba por cuenta propia, pero no como periodista. Una flâneuse. Quería su tajada. Más inquietante aún: al reconocerme como latina, se dirigió a mí en mi lengua materna.

Lo peor fue la paranoia que vino después. La próxima vez que cené sola, batallé con la duda de sacar Lolita. Me asqueaba mi cobardía.

Pero, claro que eso puede pasarte en el Barrio Rojo, piensas. Bien, déjame contarte de aquella vez en la redacción de un periódico local donde trabajaba.

Mientras andaba con prisa hacia mi escritorio, ajustaba el imperdible que fijaba la capa interior de mi blusa a la falda que heredé de los días en que mi madre trabajaba. Lo hacía con sutileza, un vistazo rápido, pero el editor de la A1 estaba atento. Debió haber estado de espaldas, pero había girado su silla.

“¿Por qué no te bajo la falda y ya?”, espetó, y yo me detuve con expresión inescrutable. Entonces supe lo que quiso decir cuando afirmó que quería trabajar conmigo. Un trueque de los más antiguos. “No”, respondí y me alejé. Nunca lo mencioné a mis colegas, y él siguió como si jamás se hubiese propasado con la periodista más joven del equipo. Por entonces, yo era la única reportera hispanohablante del periódico, algo en lo que solo reparé en retrospectiva.

En esa época trabajaba muchas horas. A menudo era parte del turno nocturno que, en la sección de las noticias locales, se reducía al editor de la A1 y a algunas almas desgraciadas que trabajaban contrarreloj. En los años siguientes, ese señor y yo colaboramos en decenas de artículos. No me quedaba de otra. No había manera de llegar a la primera plana sino a través de él.

Mis amigas me dicen que es el pelo. Ondas luminosas tan largas que se enredan en las sillas. Los hombres no pueden contenerse, es lo que insinúan. Una amiga de la secundaria me preguntó por qué no me lo cortaba. Las mujeres son las únicas que hacen tal sugerencia.

Les digo que el patriarcado insiste en que las mujeres sin acompañantes están a la venta. Además, me niego a empequeñecerme. Ocupo espacio sin pedir disculpas, y más que cualquier otro rasgo, es esta virtud la que incita al juicio. Nuestra sociedad no sabe lidiar con una mujer que mira directo a los ojos.

En estos días, me centro en bajar la vista para asegurarme de que mis pequeños no mueran. No es paranoia. Tienen la tendencia de correr hacia el peligro. Pero bueno, lo mismo hacía su madre.

Me imagino cómo me sentiría si tuviera una hija que se propusiera estudiar a las trabajadoras sexuales en el país comunista del que me había escapado justo antes de que la geopolítica atrapara a los que se quedaron. Tras un semestre de estudios en la Universidad de La Habana, estaba demasiado enfocada en regresar a Cuba para preocuparme por lo que pensaría mamá.

En el verano de 2002, la idea era dedicarme a entrevistar jineteras (la jerga cubana para referirse a las trabajadoras sexuales hace un guiño a montar a caballo) y sus clientes. Encontraría académicos, policías y políticos dispuestos a hablar. Filmaría cada entrevista y escena callejera. Llevaría a cabo mi investigación sin resultar herida, encarcelada ni deportada, pese a mi falta de estrategia para lograrlo.

Fue mi primera experiencia con el periodismo, que en aquel momento racionalicé como un aprendizaje transnacional. En La Habana, donde aún descansan los restos de mi bisabuela en un cementerio para monjas, y no para madres solteras, descubriría lo que ocurrió con las vidas de las mujeres que permanecieron en la isla mientras las demás empacamos y nos fuimos.

Obviemos las citas de mi tesis de Harvard: “Jineteras en la Habana: Constructions of Sex Worker Identity”. Me he aferrado a las palabras que me concedió —magna cum laude— como si pudieran protegerme de mi condición de mujer.

Lo que valoro me ha hecho vulnerable de maneras impredecibles. Me pasé gran parte de la vida acreditando a mi cerebro para que se me permitiera elevarme de este cuerpo y ser reconocida por mi mente. Sin embargo, como escritora he aprendido que no hay mayor sabiduría que la que emana de mi mujeridad. Pensar que casi reniego de mis vivencias para encarnar la tercera persona, para favorecer esa omnisciencia distante en la que no creo. Nuestros roces con la aniquilación son constantes, disímiles y, en su mayoría, silenciados.…

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-20 17:50 UTC

Original link: https://therumpus.net/2026/11/20/todas-sostenemos-una-llama-contra-el-viento/

item.title: Juiced to the Gills
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

You have, by now, read something about the Enhanced Games, the steroid-fueled athletic spectacle held this year in Las Vegas. (Perhaps we even recommended it.) But there’s nothing quite like seeing the event through Kent Russell’s eyes as he sneaks high-proof whiskey from his ThermoFlask, considers the physical demands of parenting and his own life’s onrushing decline, and concedes that a drug-enhanced life sounds “pretty fucking dope.”

As of this moment, the sprinters are clean, the Erth bleachers are searing the backs of my thighs, and Michael Bryan is overawing me through the act of locomotion. I sip from my thermos and bask in wonderment that a human body can be made to move that way. Beauty of this kind, which eighteenth-century types correctly filed under the category of the sublime, requires that it exceed me. A thing I could do myself is admirable; a thing that no effort of mine could ever accomplish, that lives permanently past my ceiling, is awesome in the old, strong sense of the word, in which awe is part fear, part love, part recognition that I am small and soft. The unfairness is the source of the wonder. To resent that Bryan is gifted beyond me is to resent that the thing I’m watching is beautiful, which is insane and would require that I demand the world contain nothing larger than myself.

item.description:

Everything You Need to Know About The Nightingale Adaptation

We have a teaser trailer and a first look at The Nightingale adaptation. Sony Pictures released the trailer and gave us a first look through Vanity Fair late last week. Information about this highly anticipated adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s bestseller has been trickling out.

Here’s what you need to know about the film, so far:

- The film and the book focuses on women’s resistance and mobilization against the Nazis during WWII

- Real-life sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning will play sisters on screen for the first time

- The film is produced by Reese Witherspoon and her production company, Hello Sunshine, as well as the Fanning sisters’ production company, Lewellen Pictures

- The book was a 2023 Reese’s Book Club selection

- Reese’s Book Club and Lewellen Pictures shared a first look at the film tie-in cover

- The film’s director, Michael Morris, recently worked on another adaptation: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy, the fourth film in the series, based on Helen Fielding’s novel of the same name

- March 19, 2027 marks the U.S. premiere

- The teaser, just under three minutes, emphasizes the progression of the sisters from first-hand witnesses to the war to members of the resistance

On filming a scene together and playing sisters for the first time, Dakota Fanning told Vanity Fair,

We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hannah revealed to the publication that she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her books for the screen.

“I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.”

You probably know someone who has read Hannah’s bestseller. That says it all about the popularity of her historical fiction set in Nazi-occupied France, and gives us big reason to believe the film will be an epic success.

item.title: 7 Real Portland Locations From 'Wildwood'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The creators behind the stop-motion film Wildwood took 16 years to painstakingly craft every detail of the transportive fantasy epic. Based on a book by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis, Wildwood tells the tale of a young girl named Prue whose brother is plucked from the ground by crows. Undeterred, she and her initially hapless sidekick Curtis venture into the wilderness to find him.

What follows is a surreal journey through a land where animals talk, trees are worshiped, coyotes wield cannons, and the dead returnâalbeit not always to their original forms. Interspersed throughout are recognizable landmarks from the city of Portland, Oregon, which add a sense of modernity and charm to the book and film.

I visited Portland to trace the real-world locations that found their way into Wildwood. Here are some of them.

Forest Park

Meloy and Ellis conceptualized the story on their many walks through Portlandâs Forest Park. From the first moment I spotted the wall of infinite shades of green rising up almost directly from the city streets, I could see why this place lent itself to imaginal flights of fancy.

It was a crisp autumn morning, a sheen of rain still on the ground. I had started my morning with a latte and breakfast burrito at the quaint Haven Coffee Co., so I was feeling pleasantly energized as I walked down a street lined with orange trees.Â

My guide from Around Portland Tours seemed to know everything about the area. We passed a hill overlooking a cluster of factories that provided the inspiration for the Industrial Wastes in Wildwood. They had been built on a former wetland, my guide informed me. In the book, these are a mysterious cluster of factories and warehouses that act as a barrier between Portland and the so-called Impassable Wilderness beyond.Â

Barely a minute later, we were inside another realmâa kingdom of trees. Towering Douglas firs and cedars soared towards the sky. Dewy ferns and huckleberry bushes shimmered, massive orange maple leaves coated the ground, and countless types of mushrooms covered fallen trees in the process of decomposing and becoming new life.Â

I have always felt uniquely at peace in forests, and this one was no exception; a sense of deep calm and presence washed over me immediately. Forest bathingâor the practice of wandering through a forest, exploring it with all your sensesâis an increasingly popular way to reduce stress and improve health, my guide explained, and this one felt like the perfect place to do just that.Â

The fact that the forest stood so close to bustling city streets made it feel all the more otherworldly, as if we truly had stepped through a portal from the human world into something much wilder and older.

The woods of the Pacific Northwest have long inspired various tales of cryptids such as Sasquatch, and I didnât have to look far to see withered, gnarled trunks or mossy stones that resembled various mythical creatures. This was the forestâs domain, and even human-made structures were all in the process of being reclaimed. We paused for a while at the dilapidated Witchâs Cabin, a former outpost rapidly being swallowed by moss and lichens. Altars made of stones, books, and Polaroids filled the crumbling windows.

Then we continued deeper and higher up into the woods. At one point, I caught a tiny glimpse of a house poking through the tall trees. That was the house originally used as the Cullensâ home in the first Twilight movie, my guide informed me, and indeed it wasn't too hard to imagine vampires leaping through these trees.

We continued our climb. The beauty was near-indescribable; the forest consisted of countless colors that shone far brighter in real life than in any of my photos. The air filling my lungs was clean, alive. I wanted to stay, to continue to wander through all 5,200 acres of the United Statesâ largest urban park.

The Bird Alliance

Our first stop within Forest Park was the Bird Alliance, which served as the inspiration for Wildwood's Avian Principality, or the kingdom of birds. Formerly the Audubon Society, this 150-acre expanse of land is dedicated to protecting birds and connecting people to nature.

We made our way down to a large enclosure, which I knew was home to the bird that inspired the noble Owl Rex in Wildwood. At first we couldnât spot her. The enclosure was large, filled with various perches, fauna, and equipment, and had wire mesh walls that looked out onto the forest.Â

Suddenly I realized that she had been perched on a branch directly above us the whole time, almost as if she had specifically been waiting for our appointment. Julio was a Great Horned Owl who looked remarkably regal, with round golden eyes that burned with intelligence. The plaque beside her explained she had been rescued as a young owl and never learned how to successfully be wild, which was why she spent her days here.Â

Her head swiveled backward, and she stretched out her scalloped wings for a moment. It was not hard at all to see why Meloy and Ellis had thought to model the Crown Prince of the Avian Principality after her. As we left, I felt somehow obligated to thank her for her presence. I then bought a bird-themed puzzle at a quaint gift shop, and then we ventured back into the woods.

Pittock Mansion

We then made our way up Wildwood Trail, the path that inspired the name of Meloy and Ellisâs book. The forest seemed to grow deeper and ever-wilder, until a mansion emerged out of nowhere.

It was grand, built in the French Renaissance style with smooth sandstone walls, and I recognized it immediately. I had seen the film Wildwood just two days before, and now I had the strange feeling that Iâd stepped directly into a scene from it. The experience was disorienting, as if the lines between reality and story had blurred ever-so slightly.

Pittock Mansion was built in 1914 for Oregonian publisher and businessman Henry Pittock and his wife Georgiana, a philanthropist who founded the Portland Rose Society. The mansion is rumored to be haunted by both Henry and Georgianaâs spirits, among others, and today it is preserved as a museum and event space.

We sat by the edge of the grounds, looking down over Portland and towards the towering Mount Hood, which was veiled in clouds. The mountain hasnât been as snowy as usual in recent years, my guide said, and we both were quiet for a while. I thought of the droughts and wildfires that had filled the news recently. Wildwood, I reflected, is not only about fanciful forest adventures; itâs also about human greed and violence, and the dangers of taking what does not belong to you. âWhen you mess with nature,â my guide said, using more colorful language in reality to effectively sum up one of Wildwoodâs core messages, âit messes back.â

I had thought we might walk back through the woods, but instead we made our way down a winding street that led us past a series of impressively elegant mansions, all staring out over the city. Then, all at once, we arrived at a bus station beside a bustling highway. Minutes later, we were back among the skyscrapers and gas stations of the metropolitan world.

I felt like Iâd just been somewhere secret and magical yet profoundly real and alive, and this world of humans and cars felt more like the dream. I had been entertaining the idea of leaving the city to live closer to nature for some time, and this experience, among other things, made me sure that my next home would be somewhere closer to the woods.

St. Johns Bridge

That afternoon, I made my way over towards St. Johns, the neighborhood where Meloy and Ellis lived while writing Wildwood. Rain clouds were gathering, but I had my umbrella and decided to brave it. It was drizzling when I got out near the bridge.Â…

item.title: The Most Common European Ancestry in Every State, Mapped
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country. But some states had one country's ancestors dominate over the others when it comes to where residents can trace their roots.

The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.

Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.

Germany

German immigrants have been coming to the United States since before the United States existed. A group of Quaker families arrived in 1683 and founded Germantown, which is now a suburb of Philadelphia. The largest wave, however, came in the 1800s when Germans arrived with hopes of securing land to farm or leave after a failed revolution in 1848. They brought with them things like kindergarten, the tradition of Christmas trees, and hot dogs.

Today, an estimated 40 to 60 million Americans consider German their main heritage, making it the largest country of origin for immigration. It's even more than Irish or Italian heritage and is the main European heritage in 27 states, more than any other European group. German roots are mainly found in the Midwest and West Coast.

England

Another strong country for where Americans claim roots is England. After all, England provided some of the earliest settlers across the Atlantic along the East Coast, with colonists first arriving in Jamestown in modern-day Virginia in 1607.

English roots dominate the South, with states in the Southeast claiming English heritage over all other European countries. English pockets also remain in New England, like Maine and Vermont, as well as out west in New Mexico, Utah, and Idaho.

Ireland

Irish immigration peaked in the United States in the mid-1800s, when the Great Famine ravaged the country. It's estimated that between 1851 and 1860, more than 80% of immigrants arriving in the United States came from Ireland. Additional near-famines in the second half of the 1800s propped up the flow of immigrants from Ireland to the United States.

Those migration waves left a lasting effect on the East Coast, where five states still claim Irish heritage as the most common European heritage. States where Ireland is the most represented European heritage include Delaware, the District of Columbia, and the New England states of New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. Even New York, which is known for its diverse population in New York City, cites Ireland as the country that produced the highest number of ancestral European roots among residents.

Italy

Only two states claim Italy as the most common European ancestor among their residents, with East Coast states Connecticut and New Jersey representing the country.

Italians arrived in the United States most notably in the 20th century. But while other immigrants came through New York City and moved inland, Italian immigrants stayed in the area, with an estimated one-third settling around New York City.

In New Jersey, almost 1.3 million residents claim some sort of Italian ancestry, pushing it past Irish ancestry by more than 100,000 residents.

Connecticut has a similar dynamic, with Italian heritage outnumbering Irish ancestry, and both groups clearly leading the state.

France

Louisiana is the only state that claims French ancestry more than any other European ancestry among residents.

France had already established itself in Louisiana before the 1800s, but the Louisiana Purchase solidified Louisiana's placeâand its French traditionsâin American life. The 1803 purchase included parts of several states as far as modern-day Montana and Minnesota, but Louisiana in particular held on to its French roots after the handover of land.

item.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people.

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.

A growing trend

One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.

My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion.

Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.

Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Family caregivers pay a price

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460.

But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.

Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.

Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

A ‘daughterhood penalty’

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.

But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-20 19:58 UTC

item.title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men.

That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by David Walliams, accusations Walliams denies. There was earnest discussion of the enabling power of celebrity, how stardust blinds people from seeing what’s in front of them. Some suggested the problem was narrower still, with abuse cast as a function of the way British comedy operates, lacking a recognisable HR structure or protection for junior workers from big names with clout. In parallel, a debate began about staggering the age of consent, addressing the particular dynamics of older men who target younger women, including those who would be regarded as children by any definition except the letter of the law.

All of those are valid questions, by the way. But if, underlying them, is the consoling hope that we are facing a limited problem, one confined to, say, high-status men or those whose victims are very young, then Thursday’s verdicts should dispel it. The grimmer truth is that this problem is wider and deeper: the guilty were ordinary men, carpenters and cabbies, ready to violate a middle-aged woman who was audibly and visibly unconscious.

Even this especially shocking crime – in which a man recruits other men online to rape his sedated wife – may not be as rare as we imagine. A similar case is now being tried in Manchester and, according to Wiltshire police: “This may be a significantly under-reported crime type.”

Of course, there are specific elements and contexts that make rape and sexual abuse more possible. Just as the entertainment industry provided a hospitable environment for Brand, so Philip Young could advertise for fellow rapists thanks to online forums such as Craigslist and Reddit. The internet made it easier for him to secure sedative drugs. But these things facilitate rather than drive the impulse. They are not the heart of the matter. Which is, to state it plainly, male hatred of women.

Of course, such hatred is not universal; not every man is infected by it. But it is embedded in our world and sits deep in our culture. (After Pelicot and Young, you look again at Sleeping Beauty: what exactly did we think was going on in a story that, in its 17th-century telling, had the king discover the unmoving, unconscious body of a woman, rape and impregnate that woman, and then flee?)

In Afghanistan, the Taliban have imposed gender apartheid, prohibiting girls and women from learning, singing, taking a bus without a man or walking to the park. According to Human Rights Watch, one directive ordered the removal of windows, lest Afghan women, “imprisoned in their homes, might see the outside world”. Closer to hand, you look at the manosphere, whose leading lights delight in the degradation and humiliation of women, treating their girlfriends as, at best, unpaid domestic servants or, at worst, property and chattel. You contemplate the rates of femicide, which include three women killed every fortnight in England and Wales by a current or former partner. You look at the rape statistics, including the estimate from the Centre for Women’s Justice (CWJ) that only 15% of all rapes get reported and that, of those that do, only a tiny percentage ultimately ends in a conviction.

Women have been saying all this, loudly and clearly, for years. When cases such as Brand or Walliams or Philip Young erupt, it tends to be women who lead the debate and make the arguments, in print and on the airwaves. On one level, that’s obvious – in the same way that, say, Jewish voices are given the floor when there is a murderous attack on Jews. But it’s also incomplete. Because it misses out, and risks letting off the hook, those who have most work to do. In this case, men.

The logic of that was encapsulated well by a small sign – no more than an A4 piece of paper – held up by a woman protesting in New York earlier this year over the case of the Cornell seven: the fraternity brothers at Cornell University accused of gang-raping a female student they’d incapacitated through ketamine, and doing so over the course of seven hours. The protester’s sign carried three words that had been crossed out: Protect Your Daughters. In their place were three different words: Educate Your Sons.

This shifts responsibility to where it should lie. It honours the principle articulated so concisely by Gisèle Pelicot herself who, like Joanne Young, waived her right to anonymity, believing there was no need to hide herself since she had nothing to be ashamed of. Or, as she put it, “Shame has to change sides.”

That makes moral sense, but it might make practical sense too. Take the kind of young man susceptible to the example of Andrew Tate and his fellow denizens of the manosphere. If such a man hears a woman condemn misogyny, if they hear a woman speak of the necessity of consent, they will hear those as messages that stand in opposition to manliness. They will understand their own sexual desires as manly and restraints on those desires as their opposite, as unmanly or feminine. For a man such as this, it is perhaps only condemnation by other men, framed in terms of maleness, that will cut through.

A useful precedent could be what was, in a different era, called wife-beating. Not so long ago, the culture all but countenanced such behaviour. Think of the Beatles’ song, Run For Your Life, both its title and lyric: “Well, I’d rather see you dead, little girl / Than to be with another man”. But attitudes moved. “The norm did shift,” CWJ founder Harriet Wistrich told me on Friday. These days, if a man were hitting his partner in sight of another man, that second man would, she hopes, step in.

This, then, is how fathers might best heed that protester’s call to educate their sons. To tell them that the kind of behaviour that has been revealed in courtrooms and on front pages these last two weeks is wicked and inhuman, but also pathetic, inadequate and weak – and, yes, worthy of shame. That to prey on those who have less power, or no power at all, is the mark of someone who is not merely a failure as a person – but no man at all.

- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

item.title: Did men evolve to fight each other? Scientists can’t agree.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court. While eating a cheeseburger, he overheard two men behind him speaking in unusually deep voices. “I turned around to see what was happening, and there was a young, good-looking female nearby,” Puts said.

His initial thought was that human males evolved deep voices to attract women, but he soon began to wonder whether they might also help establish dominance over other men: “A deep voice is intimidating — think about Darth Vader.” So, for his dissertation, Puts tested both possibilities. What he found surprised him.

Women tended to prefer a deeper, more masculine voice, but the effect of voice pitch on their ratings of male attractiveness wasn’t very big. Meanwhile, the effect of voice pitch on men’s judgment of another man’s dominance and fighting ability was 15 times bigger.

The unexpected result led Puts to revisit earlier studies. He noticed that “the literature was really biased towards female mate choice” as a reason for deep voices, while findings related to male-male competition seemed to get “pushed under the rug.” This realization became the foundation for Puts’ theory that competition between males for mates, also known as “male-male contest competition,” may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized.

Puts, now a professor of anthropology and psychology at Pennsylvania State University, has continued to think about and develop this theory ever since the seed for it was planted in his brain in that mall food court in the early 2000s. Although he said he is mostly driven by a fascination with human nature, there’s more to his theory than pure academic interest. He believes that evolutionary understanding might help explain aspects of male psychology and inform positive social change.

Competition between males for mates may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized.

In November 2026, Puts and graduate student Saeed Koohgard published a review titled “The deadliest primate: Contest competition and the evolution of human males” in the Journal of Human Evolution. The review links modern-day male characteristics, including physical aggression, to male-male contest competition among our ancestors — a controversial theory.

Grateful for curious minds

This Thanksgiving, get 15% off Big Think membership and join a community of idea explorers. Use code BIGTHANKS15 at checkout. Valid on annual plans for new members only.

“This [idea] is supported primarily by evolutionary psychologists,” said Agustín Fuentes, an anthropologist at Princeton University. “Most anthropologists do not support this at all.” He said that those interested in understanding male violence should read the paper “but recognize this is a very teeny slice and a very biased view” in the midst of the wider anthropological, psychological, and sociological literature.

The ancestral mating system

For at least the past 150,000 years, the effective number of reproducing women at any given time has been roughly three times that of men, according to a 2015 study looking at Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA. This may reflect male invaders displacing local men, but Puts and Koohgard think it points to a polygynous mating system, where some men fathered children with several partners, while many other men had no children at all. They believe that our ancestors lived in single-male family units embedded within larger bands, as hamadryas and gelada baboons do.

This setup meant that “our male ancestors intensely fought, threatened, and killed each other to monopolize mates,” Puts said.

In their review, Puts and Koohgard cite several findings that are consistent with their theory. For example, in a study of Eurasian Neanderthal and early modern human remains from 80,000 to 20,000 years ago, men were about six times more likely than women to show signs of head injuries. Furthermore, a study of homicide data spanning two decades and four locations (Canada, England/Wales, Chicago, and Detroit) found that unrelated men kill each other 27 times more often than unrelated women kill each other.

“A lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

David Puts

Puts and Koohgard also point to several features of the male anatomy as complementary evidence of male-male contest competition. Men are larger than women on average, with 61% more muscle mass overall and 75% more upper-body muscle mass. Size and muscularity are traits that help win fights. Men also have what biologists call “badges of status,” such as facial hair and deep voices. These traits signal dominance and help to win resources, such as mates, without engaging in costly fights.

Puts and Koohgard argue that, together, these lines of evidence suggest that male-male contest competition has played an important role in shaping men’s behaviors, including physical aggression. People might hear this theory and misread it as a justification of male violence, Puts said, but he stresses that understanding evolutionary influences is not the same as condoning violence — the idea that something being natural or evolved makes it justified is what’s known as the “naturalistic fallacy.”

Although Puts and Koohgard’s theory centers on the idea that aggression helped our male ancestors to win mates, Puts doubts that the most violent males were ever the most successful. “There are huge costs to violence,” he said, “and if you’re living in a group and you’re a belligerent loose cannon, you’re likely to be killed or at least ostracized.” Instead, Puts thinks that “a lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

Clashing views

Fuentes is not convinced by Puts and Koohgard’s theory. The claim of a polygynous ancestral mating system is “highly disputed,” he said, and the “vast majority of geneticists who work in this area” conclude that our ancestors were most likely monogamous, with some mild polygyny.

He accused Puts and Koohgard of selectively citing works that support their theory while leaving out research that complicates or challenges it — their paper doesn’t mention Nam Kim and Marc Kissel’s book Emergent Warfare in Our Evolutionary Past, for example. That book frames violence as complex and dependent on multiple conditions — not simply an evolved male strategy. Citing it would make it “more complicated to make the argument that [they’re] making,” Fuentes said.

However, Raymond Hames, an emeritus professor of anthropology at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, praised Puts and Koohgard’s review as “very comprehensive.” He said the paper’s strength is that it tests several alternative hypotheses that might explain male traits, such as sexual division of labor, and finds them a poor fit. His only objection is to the paper’s title: “The deadliest primate.” “Although we are violent, we are not the deadliest of all primates,” Hames said. Red-tailed monkeys, blue monkeys, and red-fronted lemurs are all far more likely than humans to kill their own kind, according to a 2016 study.

“Humans didn’t evolve to punch each other — our hands are horrible at it. Our bodies actually aren’t that great for violence, but our minds are.”

Agustín Fuentes

With regard to Fuentes’ point, Hames thinks that warfare, or coalitionary violence, and one-on-one male violence aren’t interchangeable. One involves political competition over scarce resources, he said, while “the other one has to do with males striving for reproduction.”…

Source: Big Think | Published: 2026-11-20 16:00 UTC

item.title: 20 Different Ways To Say “I Know” and “I Understand”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Do you often say “I know” or “I understand” in English?

These expressions are perfectly correct, but native English speakers use lots of other phrases to show that they know something, understand an explanation, or recognize what someone is talking about.

And be careful – some expressions can sound friendly and enthusiastic, while others might sound impatient or even rude!

In this lesson, you’ll learn 20 natural English expressions you can use instead of “I know” and “I understand” – as well as their opposites, “I don’t know” and “I don’t understand.” Some are casual, some are idioms, and some have slightly different meanings depending on the situation.

Different Ways to Say “I Know”

1. I’m aware of that.

This means you already know a particular fact or piece of information. It’s a little more formal than simply saying “I know.”

Example:

- A: “The deadline for submitting the application is Friday.”

- B: “Yes, I’m aware of that. I’m planning to submit mine tomorrow.”

Be careful with your tone of voice! If you say “I’m aware of that” in an annoyed tone, it can sound like you’re irritated that someone is telling you something you already know.

2. I heard about that.

Use this when someone tells you some news, but you’ve already received that information from another source.

Example:

- A: “Did you know they’re opening a new shopping mall downtown?”

- B: “Yeah, I heard about that! Apparently, it’s going to have over 100 stores.”

This expression is especially common when talking about news, recent events, and things that are happening in your community.

3. I’m familiar with that.

This means you have some knowledge or experience of a subject, person, or thing.

- A: “Have you ever used this software?”

- B: “Yes, I’m familiar with it. We used it at my previous company.”

4. I’m well aware.

This is an emphatic way to say you already know something. Depending on your tone of voice, it can sound a little annoyed.

- A: “You still have a lot of work to finish.”

- B: “I’m well aware. I’ve been working on it all morning.”

5. I know it by heart.

This means you’ve memorized something so well that you can repeat it without looking.

- A: “Do you need the address?”

- B: “No, I know it by heart. I’ve been there dozens of times.”

Different Ways to Say “I Understand”

6. I see.

This is one of the simplest and most common ways to show that you understand what someone is explaining.

Example:

- A: “We can’t start construction until we get the necessary permits.”

- B: “I see. So we’ll have to wait a few more weeks.”

You can also say “Oh, I see!” when you suddenly understand something that wasn’t clear before.

7. Got it! / Gotcha

This is a short, informal way to say you understand instructions or information.

Example:

- A: “When you get to the building, take the elevator to the third floor and turn right.”

- B: “Got it! Thanks!”

You might also hear “I’ve got it” or “Gotcha!” in casual conversation.

“Got it” is especially useful when someone is giving you directions or explaining what you need to do.

8. That makes sense.

Use this expression when you understand the logic or reasoning behind something.

Example:

- A: “We’re moving the meeting to the afternoon because several people are unavailable in the morning.”

- B: “That makes sense. I’ll update my calendar.”

This phrase doesn’t just mean you understand the information – it also suggests that the explanation seems reasonable to you.

9. I get the picture.

This means you understand the general situation, even if you don’t know every detail.

- A: “The supplier was late, two employees called in sick, and then our computer system stopped working…”

- B: “Okay, I get the picture. You’ve had a really stressful day.”

10. I hear you.

This is an informal expression that means you understand someone’s feelings, concerns, or frustrations.

Example:

- A: “I’m exhausted. It feels like there’s never enough time to get everything done.”

- B: “I hear you. You’ve had a lot on your plate lately.”

Notice that “I hear you” doesn’t simply mean you can physically hear the other person’s voice. Instead, it means you’re listening and you understand how they feel.

It’s especially useful when someone is complaining, expressing frustration, or talking about a difficult situation.

Different Ways to Say “I Don’t Know”

Now let’s look at five more interesting ways to say you don’t know something.

11. Beats me!

This is a very casual way to say you have absolutely no idea.

Example:

- A: “Why is the internet so slow today?”

- B: “Beats me! It was working fine this morning.”

“Beats me” is short, informal, and common in everyday conversations. You wouldn’t normally use it in a formal business email.

12. Your guess is as good as mine.

This expression means you don’t know the answer, and the other person has just as much chance of guessing correctly as you do.

Example:

- A: “When do you think they’ll announce the results?”

- B: “Your guess is as good as mine. They haven’t given us a date.”

It’s often used when both people are uncertain about something.

13. No clue / I don’t have a clue.

This is an emphatic way to say you have absolutely no idea.

Example:

- A: “Do you know where I left my keys?”

- B: “I don’t have a clue. Have you checked your jacket pockets?”

A clue is a piece of information that helps you solve a mystery or find an answer.

So if you haven’t got a clue, you don’t have any information that would help you answer the question.

You can also say “I have no clue” or simply “No clue!”

14. Don’t ask me!

This is an informal expression used when you don’t know the answer, often with a slightly amused, surprised, or frustrated tone.

Example:

- A: “Why does the printer keep breaking?”

- B: “Don’t ask me! I can barely get it to work myself.”

Be careful: depending on your tone of voice, “Don’t ask me!” can sound a little rude or impatient.

It’s best used in casual conversations with people you know well.

15. Who knows?

This is a casual, conversational way to say you don’t know the answer, especially when something is uncertain or difficult to predict.

Example:

- A: “Do you think they’ll lower prices next year?”

- B: “Who knows? They might, but I wouldn’t count on it.”

Although it’s phrased as a question, “Who knows?” isn’t usually asking someone to identify a person who knows the answer. It’s simply expressing uncertainty.

You can also say “Who knows!” with a more enthusiastic tone when talking about exciting possibilities:

- “Maybe I’ll get the job. Who knows!”

Different Ways to Say “I Don’t Understand”

Finally, let’s learn five expressions you can use when something is confusing or difficult to understand.

16. I’m not following.

This is a natural, polite way to say you’re having trouble understanding someone’s explanation.

Example:

- A: “First, we multiply the total by the percentage, then subtract that amount from the original number.”

- B: “Sorry, I’m not following. Could you explain that again?”

You can also say “I’m not sure I follow.”

This is especially useful in meetings, classes, and other situations where you want someone to clarify what they’re saying.

17. You’ve lost me.

This means you were following someone’s explanation at first, but then you became confused.

Example:

- A: “So we transfer the data to the second system, which automatically updates the third database…”

- B: “Wait, you’ve lost me. Why do we need three different systems?”

The idea is that you were mentally following the person, but at some point you couldn’t keep up anymore.

It’s a very natural expression when someone is explaining something complicated.

18. I can’t wrap my head around it.

This idiom means something is extremely difficult for you to understand or accept.

Example:

- A: “The company made record profits last year, but now they’re laying off hundreds of employees.”

- B: “I can’t wrap my head around it. That makes no sense.”

You can also use this expression for complicated concepts:

- “I’ve been studying this math problem for an hour, but I still can’t wrap my head around it.”…

Source: Espresso English | Published: 2026-11-20 18:57 UTC

item.title: 33 Common English Words With Multiple Meanings
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Many common English words have several completely different meanings!

For example, the word fine can mean something is good, but it can also mean a penalty you have to pay. And the word charge can mean asking someone for money, putting electricity into a battery, or officially accusing someone of a crime!

This is one of the reasons English vocabulary can be tricky. Even if you know a word, you might not recognize it when it’s used in a different context.

In today’s lesson, you’ll learn 33 common English words with 3 different meanings each – that’s 99 meanings in total! Each meaning comes with an example sentence to help you understand how the word is used in real life.

Everyday Words with Surprising Meanings

These are words you probably already know, but they have some additional meanings that might surprise you!

1. FINE

Meaning 1: Good, acceptable, or satisfactory

- Don’t worry about me. I’m fine.

Meaning 2: Money that must be paid as punishment for breaking a rule or law

- She had to pay a $100 fine for speeding.

Meaning 3: Very thin, small, or delicate

- The artist used a fine brush to paint the tiny details.

2. BREAK

Meaning 1: To damage something so that it stops working or separates into pieces

- Be careful not to break your phone!

Meaning 2: A short period of rest

- Let’s take a 15-minute break before continuing.

Meaning 3: An opportunity, especially one that leads to success

- He got his big break when a famous director offered him a role.

3. SPOT

Meaning 1: A particular place or location

- This is my favorite spot to sit and read.

Meaning 2: A small mark, stain, or area of a different color

- There’s a spot of coffee on your shirt.

Meaning 3: To notice or recognize something

- Can you spot the difference between these two pictures?

4. MISS

Meaning 1: To feel sad because someone is absent

- I really miss my family when I’m traveling.

Meaning 2: To fail to catch or reach something

- I missed the bus and had to wait another 20 minutes.

Meaning 3: To fail to attend or experience something

- I missed yesterday’s meeting because I was sick.

5. PASS

Meaning 1: To successfully complete a test or examination

- She passed her driving test on the first try.

Meaning 2: To give something to another person

- Could you pass me the salt, please?

Meaning 3: To decline an opportunity or offer

- Thanks for inviting me, but I think I’ll pass this time.

6. FIT

Meaning 1: To be the correct size or shape

- These jeans don’t fit me anymore.

Meaning 2: Healthy and physically strong

- My grandfather is still very fit at the age of 80.

Meaning 3: A sudden period of strong emotion or uncontrolled behavior

- The child threw a fit when his parents said he couldn’t have any candy.

7. SOUND

Meaning 1: Something you hear; a noise

- I heard a strange sound coming from the kitchen.

Meaning 2: To seem or appear a certain way based on what you hear

- That sounds like a great idea!

Meaning 3: Reliable, sensible, or based on good judgment

- My father always gives me sound advice.

8. MATTER

Meaning 1: To be important

- It doesn’t matter what other people think.

Meaning 2: A subject, situation, or problem

- We need to discuss an important matter before the meeting ends.

Meaning 3: Physical substance

- Everything around us is made of matter.

9. POINT

Meaning 1: An idea or argument expressed in a discussion

- You made a good point about the cost of the project.

Meaning 2: The purpose or reason for doing something

- What’s the point of buying a new phone if your old one still works?

Meaning 3: To indicate a person, place, or thing with your finger

- She pointed to the building across the street.

10. CASE

Meaning 1: A particular situation or example

- In this case, I think we should make an exception.

Meaning 2: A legal matter investigated or decided by a court

- The lawyer has been working on this case for months.

Meaning 3: A container used to protect or carry something

- I bought a protective case for my new laptop.

11. CHECK

Meaning 1: To examine something to make sure it’s correct or working properly

- Please check your answers before submitting the test.

Meaning 2: The bill at a restaurant (American English)

- Could we have the check, please?

Meaning 3: A written order instructing a bank to pay money from someone’s account

- She wrote a check to pay the rent.

Common Verbs with Multiple Uses

These everyday verbs are extremely useful because they can express many different actions and ideas depending on the context.

12. RUN

Meaning 1: To move quickly on foot

- I run three miles every morning before work.

Meaning 2: To manage or operate a business or organization

- She runs a small business from her home.

Meaning 3: To function or operate (a machine or system)

- My computer is running much faster since I installed the update.

13. SET

Meaning 1: To put something in a particular place or position

- She set her bag on the floor and sat down.

Meaning 2: To establish or decide something, such as a date, goal, or rule

- We’ve set a deadline for completing the project.

Meaning 3: A group or collection of similar or related things

- My parents gave us a new set of dishes for our wedding.

14. DRAW

Meaning 1: To create a picture using a pencil, pen, or other tool

- My daughter loves to draw animals.

Meaning 2: To attract attention or interest

- The unusual advertisement drew a lot of attention.

Meaning 3: To finish a competition with equal scores

- The two teams drew 2–2.

15. COVER

Meaning 1: To put something over another thing

- Cover the pot and let the soup cook for 20 minutes.

Meaning 2: To include or discuss a particular subject

- Today’s lesson covers 33 common English words.

Meaning 3: To pay for something

- Don’t worry about dinner tonight. I’ll cover the bill.

16. PICK

Meaning 1: To choose or select something

- You can pick whichever restaurant you like.

Meaning 2: To collect fruit, flowers, or vegetables from where they grow

- We went to a farm to pick strawberries.

Meaning 3: To remove something using your fingers or a pointed object

- She carefully picked a piece of glass out of her shoe.

17. HOLD

Meaning 1: To carry or keep something in your hands

- Could you hold my bag for a minute?

Meaning 2: To organize or conduct an event or meeting

- The company will hold its annual conference in June.

Meaning 3: To remain true, valid, or effective

- The same rule holds for everyone, regardless of their position.

18. DROP

Meaning 1: To accidentally let something fall

- I dropped my phone on the sidewalk.

Meaning 2: To decrease or become lower

- Temperatures are expected to drop below freezing tonight.

Meaning 3: To stop doing or participating in something

- He decided to drop the course because he didn’t have enough time.

19. RAISE

Meaning 1: To lift or move something to a higher position

- Please raise your hand if you have a question.

Meaning 2: To increase an amount, price, or level

- The company plans to raise its prices next month.

Meaning 3: To take care of a child as they grow up

- She was raised by her grandparents.

20. TURN

Meaning 1: To move something around a central point or change direction

- Turn the handle to open the door.

Meaning 2: To become or change into a different state

- The leaves turn yellow and orange in the fall.

Meaning 3: An opportunity to do something in a sequence

- It’s your turn to choose a movie.

21. SERVE

Meaning 1: To provide food or drinks

- The restaurant serves breakfast until 11 AM.

Meaning 2: To perform a role, duty, or official position

- She served on the school board for five years.

Meaning 3: To be useful for a particular purpose

- The spare bedroom also serves as my home office.

22. BACK

Meaning 1: The rear part of something

- There’s a small garden at the back of the house.

Meaning 2: To support or agree with someone

- I think it’s a great idea, and I’ll back you all the way.

Meaning 3: To provide financial support for a project or business

- Several investors agreed to back the new company.

Words Used in Work, News, and Formal Contexts…

Source: Espresso English | Published: 2026-11-20 18:16 UTC

item.title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

item.title: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos, recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off. Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina. Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

item.title: Josh Hazlewood suggests he could quit if any action taken against Pat Cummins over ‘sandpapergate’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Josh Hazlewood has thrown his full support behind Pat Cummins, denying they knew anything about “sandpapergate” while suggesting he could quit if any action was taken against the embattled Australian Test captain.

Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.

Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.

Cummins strenuously denied being aware of what was going on in a press conference last week, but his position has been called into question since Bancroft backed Khawaja’s version of events.

In his first comments since the story blew up, Hazlewood reiterated that the bowling group at the time, which also included Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, were not part of the plan.

They jointly released a statement in 2021 denying any involvement.

“I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood said in an interview with the Daily Telegraph.

“To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again – I think is just a remarkable job.

“He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.

“I think if we turned up for the first Test [against New Zealand in December] and he wasn’t the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don’t know how that would go.”

Asked if he would consider quitting in protest if Cummins was removed, Hazlewood said: “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah.”

Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening its investigation and chief executive Todd Greenberg has backed Cummins.

Reports said the governing body was expected to reinforce its support of him this weekend ahead of the naming of the Test squad for the New Zealand series.

“Two things stand out for me from what’s been said,” added Hazlewood.

“Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field?

“The answer is no. When it boils down to it I think those two points are crucial.”

The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner.

After Cummins’ denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a 4,000-word statement by also claiming “it was the whole team” while saying he felt “angry and betrayed” by the Test skipper.

Starc has also reinforced that he knew nothing in recent days. Lyon and Smith have yet to comment.

item.title: Price beats Kotaskova to become undisputed champion
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Price beats Kotaskova to become undisputed champion

- Published

Lauren Price dominated Michaela Kotaskova to seal her place in history by becoming undisputed world welterweight champion.

Price, 32, took an unanimous, shut-out decision and the acclaim of the crowd to add the WBO title to her collection and become the first Welsh fighter to claim the accolade of holding all four major world titles.

Already an Olympic champion and world champion from her amateur days, it further underlined her claim as being among the very best in boxing.

But the way in which she did it, extending a perfect professional record to 11 wins from her 11 fights, suggested there could yet be more to come.

Price won every round from every judge in front of a partisan Cardiff crowd, producing an unrelenting pace that punished her opponent at every opportunity.

Although Price could not force a stoppage, there was never any doubt she had done enough against an opponent full of stamina and stubbornness.

Kotaskova, beaten only once, but never stopped in her career, showed real heart but had no answer to Price's expertise.

The Tokyo gold medal winner could celebrate even before the final bell sounded, climbing the corner ropes and into the record books.

It was lapped up by a sell-out Utilita Arena crowd who excitedly acknowledged the achievement and the moment.

Wales has produced 14 world champions, some of them genuine greats.

They include, of course, Joe Calzaghe who so often graced this venue with successful defence after successful defence of his super-middleweight crown.

He never reached undisputed status, though he was able to cross the capital city to go from arena to stadium champion.

That is the next challenge for Price, claiming before she left the ring that more is to come while talk immediately turned to five-weight world champion Claressa Shields as a stadium fight next summer.

Champions recognise champions

That is for the future, but this was a night for history - with the calibre of some of the former boxers in the stands a nod to that.

Champions know champions. Five Welsh world title winners were in the capital to watch their compatriot do something never been done before.

From Cinderella Man Steve Robinson and Barry Jones, to the more recent Joe Cordina, who may still be eyeing a stadium return of his own in the coming weeks.

All have been proud to fly the flag, but perhaps none have worn it quite as much on their sleeve - or shorts - as Price has done.

Here, entering to the strains of a Welsh male voice choir, the atmosphere moved from Friday night in a city centre to full-blooded patriotism.

The anthem stirred so much Kotaskova couldn't help but raise an eyebrow before stepping out of her corner.

From then, she had no time to savour the moment let alone consider become an opportunity the Czech Republic's first world champion.

She felt flurries of punches from the first moments and struggled with the unrelenting pace set by the champion.

Steely-eyed, Price refused to allow a breath and, while Kotaskova continued to try and come onto the front foot, she was met by angry, but calculated attacks.

Kotaskova's problems only increased when she was cut in the fifth round, the hooks from the home fighter providing no let up.

At one point in the seventh, Kotaskova took a shot so fierce she almost turned her back to say no more, but still she came and still Price went hunting with hooks.

She could not find the decisive blow, finally letting the tempo slip, and even enjoying the final seconds as she accepted she had done more than enough to win and win a place in boxing history.

Edwards impresses in significant undercard win

Price was not the only Welsh winner on the night as Rhys Edwards secured a significant victory over Lee McGregor, taking an unanimous decision to claim the WBA Continental featherweight championship.

McGregor, 29, had stepped back down to featherweight after two defeats in his last three bouts and had made it clear he knew his chances of returning to world-challenging level was on the line.

His determination to keep coming forward showed what it meant, soaking up several clean shots, but Edwards proved too quick and too sharp.

The 26-year-old from Penygraig also had something to prove after a disappointing draw with Gully Powar last time out.

Then he faded in the latter round, but here Edwards managed to take McGregor's punches and maintain his own pace. It ensured what is perhaps the biggest win of his career, and to leave McGregor contemplating his options.

Elsewhere on the undercard, Willy Gilheaney's unbeaten record was taken away by the experience of Argentinean Alberto Igancio Palmetta, the former Olympic boxer showing plenty of know-how to overcome the Swansea fighter's guts and early control to take an unanimous points win.

Earlier in the night, Doncaster's Jake Goodwin took the decision in a game middleweight bout with Liverpool fighter Sean Arkwright. Goodwin â who had former world featherweight champion Josh Warrington in his corner â had only accepted the fight on two weeks' notice, accepting before he was even granted time off work.

And there were wins for Welsh fighters Brandon Scott and Kane Shepherd, while Cardigan's Josh Mellor and Newport's Lewis Howells fought to a draw.

Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears Â£100m

- Published

Manchester United borrowed another Â£10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay Â£7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.

United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed Â£10m on 16 November.

The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to Â£240m.

The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to Â£95m. However, that figure is likely to top Â£100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.

Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.

Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.

The club also confirmed they had spent Â£5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".

The filing also revealed they owe Â£417m in outstanding transfer fees, Â£181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was Â£577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.
