item.title: Alta Rock Carvings in Alta, Norway
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

About

One of the most extraordinary attractions in northern Norway is Alta Museum's outdoor area, where thousands of prehistoric carvings can be found. These are not paintings or replicas displayed behind glass – they are original artworks carved directly into the bedrock by people thousands of years ago.

Some of the carvings date back more than 7,000 years, making them among the oldest and most significant examples of prehistoric rock art in Northern Europe. They depict reindeer, bears, elk, fish, whales, boats, hunting scenes, fishing activities, human figures and mysterious rituals. The carvings were originally made near the shoreline, and as the land gradually rose after the last Ice Age, new rock surfaces became available for successive generations of artists.

Light plays an important role in discovering the carvings. Depending on the direction and angle of the sunlight, the engraved lines can become much more visible or almost disappear completely. Low-angle sunlight, especially in the morning or evening, creates small shadows inside the carved grooves, making the figures stand out more clearly.

Some of the carvings have been painted red to make them easier to see. This red colour is not original to the carvings, but was added in 1970s to help visitors recognise their shapes and details. Today, the focus is on protecting the original rock carvings while keeping modern alterations to a minimum. As part of this conservation work, the red paint is gradually being removed to preserve the site's authenticity

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised in 1985 for its outstanding cultural and historical importance.

Know Before You Go

After paying the Alta Museum admission fee, you can explore the area independently by following wooden walkways that wind through the landscape. Please note that the carvings are only accessible during the snow-free season.

The museum also has an indoor area showcasing local history.

item.title: Nevada Parents Push Lawmakers for 45-Minute Daily Recess in Elementary Schools
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Nevada Parents Push Lawmakers for 45-Minute Daily Recess in Elementary Schools

The opportunity to play, to move and to be outside should not be limited, argue supporters of the national “Say Yes to Recess” movement.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

The first time her daughter came home saying she’d missed recess for “study hall,” Brandi Vesco thought nothing of it. But as it continued to happen, she began to see skipped recess as a bigger problem.

Vesco found out the school was keeping kids from recess if they hadn’t finished their in-class work. On Wednesdays, the entire school skipped recess for additional instructional time.

When Vesco complained to the teacher and principal, they began allowing her daughter to go to recess and sending unfinished classwork home. Vesco eventually decided to enroll her daughter at a different public school, 5 minutes away, that gives students 45 minutes of recess each day.

She’d found a solution for her daughter, but one thought lingered: What about all the other kids?

“Children don’t thrive sitting and trying to learn for long periods of time,” said Vesco, a former ed-tech reporter and the founder of Washoe Parents Coalition. “It’s common sense to me. We all do better with some exercise and movement in our day.”

Vesco and the coalition are now advocating that all elementary students receive at least 45 minutes of recess during the school day. They also want to prohibit the withholding of recess for academic or minor disciplinary reasons.

They have secured a bipartisan duo of lawmakers — Assemblymembers Alexis Hansen (R-Sparks) and Selena La Rue Hatch (D-Reno) — to sponsor a bill on the issue when the Nevada State Legislature meets next year.

Hansen, in a statement to the Nevada Current, said the legislation is a “commonsense, bipartisan effort” that will promote “healthier, happier students who are better prepared to learn.”

“Recess isn’t a luxury for children,” she continued. “It’s essential to their physical, emotional, and academic development. Every Nevada elementary school student deserves time during the school day to get outside, move, play, and recharge.”

Currently, Nevada law does not require elementary schools to provide any recess time. The Nevada Department of Agriculture’s Nevada School Wellness Policy, which schools that participate in the National School Lunch Program are supposed to adopt, states schools “must provide the opportunity for moderate to vigorous physical activity” for at least 30 minutes during each regular school day. That same policy states that schools shall not withhold opportunities for physical activity as punishment.

Vesco suspects the policy has little teeth, big loopholes, or both. The coalition has been calling on parents to report existing violations of that policy to the state Department of Agriculture or Washoe County School District, which formally adopted the wellness policy.

WCSD did not respond to the Current’s request for comment.

The coalition assembled a group of volunteers to call every WCSD elementary school to determine how much recess kids were receiving.

They gathered information from 58 of the district’s 66 elementary schools and found that 14 give students 45 minutes or more of recess. They also found that schools in low-income neighborhoods have fewer minutes of recess than schools in higher-income neighborhoods. Low-income schools are also far more likely to not have a physical education teacher.

The opportunity to play, to move and to be outside should not be limited to only certain neighborhoods, argues Vesco and other supporters of the national “Say Yes to Recess” movement. Recess is a valuable part of the educational environment, offering space for friendship and connection, problem solving and resilience.

“I think our school districts get so caught up on catching kids up on their proficiencies, which we should be doing, that we end up cutting things like recess,” said La Rue Hatch, a public school teacher and mother to an elementary schooler. “But every study actually shows us that if we are taking away their recess time, we’re actually taking away their ability to focus and their ability to learn, and we’re actually going to have significantly more harmful consequences as a result.”

While the coalition is based on Washoe, they believe limiting recess is a broader problem for the state. According to Vesco, initial calls to elementary schools within Clark County School District have revealed many offer 20 minutes or less each day. In Douglas County School District, recess time varies from 30 to 55 minutes.

But it’s not all school districts. In Carson City School District, every elementary school offers 45 minutes.

The coalition believes every school can incorporate 45 minutes of recess without making their school day longer or needing additional funding.

“It’s about scheduling,” said Vesco.

The language of the “Say Yes To Recess” bill has not yet been drafted. But the Nevada Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Children’s Advocacy Alliance, and Nevada Cancer Coalition have already signed onto the cause. Vesco says other groups, including the Nevada State Education Association, which represents teachers and staff across the state, have also signaled support.

Advocates point to research showing that early elementary students who got 45 minutes of recess were “less off task and more focused in class” than students who got 30 minutes.

While the effort is still in its infancy, Vesco says initial response from parents and the public has been wildly positive: “Most people are like ‘Duh.’ Of course elementary school students can’t be sitting still without movement’” for long stretches.

Reporter Jeniffer Solis contributed to this article.

item.title: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

But the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Burnham rejected suggestions there was any confusion over the deals coming into force: “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” he said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.

Hailing the “historic” agreement Burnham said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe,” as he argued that the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

The prime minister said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, while also reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal. The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those might be. It will be to inform the next parliament.”

Burnham also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who was in Brussels on Friday to hold a retaliatory press conference, to justify why they would reject a deal which, he said, would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity. “Why would anybody turn their back on that?”

The prime minister said the deals, which were initiated by Keir Starmer, would add 0.5% to British GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Farage said Burnham had been naive and the EU had “used this moment to strongarm the British prime minister over tuition fee cuts for hundreds of thousands of EU students”.

EU leaders sought to play down differences over tuition fees. “We are heading in the same direction and that is what matters,” the European Council president, António Costa, said of the broad relationship. He described the UK as “our closest neighbour, a reliable ally and a natural partner”.

Von der Leyen said it was up to the UK to decide where the journey was going, adding: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

In a sign of tension in the negotiations, the EU agreed a declaration that the three deals would not come into force without equal treatment on fees for EU students at British universities.

“The [EU] Council and [European] Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students,” stated the confidential statement seen by the Guardian. The EU would not adopt the three agreements before “the conclusions of the negotiations … providing for equal treatment on tuition fees”, it added.

Another potential flashpoint could be the UK’s status as a rule-taker. The food and drink and emissions trading deals require the UK to align with EU rules. British experts will be invited to relevant EU meetings, including dealing with potential animal health emergencies. But Britain will not have voting rights. Burnham rejected suggestions this was a fig leaf, saying it would be “quite a moment” to have British experts back in EU meeting rooms.

France was said to be instrumental in shaping Britain’s exclusion, although Paris argues its position was widely supported and reflects the reality that a non-member state cannot be a decision-maker.

Following the talks, Burnham was invited to a lunch of pea and mint soup, battered North Sea cod and chips, followed by Brussels waffle with fruit.

The summit began with a highly choreographed welcome ceremony in the Europa “space egg” European Council building, where a quintet played the British and EU anthems.

The UK hailed a joint decision to create a “partnership for economic resilience”, as an answer to its concerns over the EU’s Made in Europe plans. The EU is still finalising legislation that will give EU companies preference when public money is spent on the key technologies, such as renewables and electric cars. The UK has been arguing for Britain to be included in Made in Europe to ensure UK firms are not locked out of European supply chains.

In response, the two sides agreed to set up “a common prosperity and economic security space”, essentially an answer to shared concerns about artificially cheap Chinese goods that are depressing prices across Europe. But questions over whether the UK needs to align with EU trade defences remain open. Burnham said the two sides had reached an agreement “to work together where we have common threats”.

In an echo of the Brexit years, the final deal emerged after late-night talks went to the wire.

The German Social Democrat MEP Bernd Lange called on both sides to resolve the tuition fees issue to make studying affordable in a way that works for universities: “We can’t open the door to young people and then price them out of walking through it.”

The EU has welcomed Burnham’s breaking of taboos over rejoining, but also voiced frustration at British negotiating tactics. “The UK has a tendency to make even small questions so difficult,” an EU diplomat said. “A British prime minister talks about a change of approach … Then in negotiations it seems like British negotiators act the same way they always had.”

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-20 17:57 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-youth-mobility-deals-biggest-step-towards-eu-since-brexit

item.title: Indianapolis Public Schools Proposes Closing 6 Schools Amid Declining Enrollment and Budget Shortfall
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Indianapolis Public Schools Proposes Closing 6 Schools Amid Declining Enrollment and Budget Shortfall

School closures would take place next summer, and could force families to adjust their plans for the 2027-28 school year.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

Indianapolis Public Schools is proposing to close six schools after this school year as student enrollment plunges and budget problems plague the district.

The following schools would be affected, according to information shared at a Tuesday agenda review session of the IPS school board, which is expected to take action on the plan Dec. 8.

- Ralph Waldo Emerson School 58. The school will merge with Christian Park School 82 at Christian Park. Christian Park will continue to offer the Exploratory instructional model.

- Robert Lee Frost School 106. The school will merge with Eliza Blaker School 55 at Eliza Blaker, which will continue to offer the Reggio-inspired instructional model.

- Benjamin Harrison School 2. The school will merge with Charity Dye School 27, which will continue to offer the International Baccalaureate (IB) instructional model.

- Longfellow Middle School. The school will merge with Howe Middle School, which will continue to offer the IB model.

- Frederick Douglass School 19 and James A. Garfield School 31 will both merge with Eleanor Skillen School 34. Eleanor Skillen will offer the STEM instructional model that James A. Garfield currently offers.

- Margaret McFarland Learning Academy (MMLA) and Positive Supports Academy will move to James A. Garfield School 31. MMLA will continue to support students with disabilities, while Positive Supports Academy will continue to offer alternative education services.

- The elementary high-ability program will move from Merle Sidener Academy 59 to the Benjamin Harrison School 2 building, which Johnson described as more central in the district.

- The new Joyce Kilmer 69 building currently under construction will become the CITY (Central Indiana Training for Youth) Career Center.

School closures would take place next summer, and could force families to adjust their plans for the 2027-28 school year — the first round of enrollment for that year closes Dec. 18. Closures would disrupt students’ plans and educational trajectories, and some might choose to leave the district altogether rather than move to another IPS school.

If the schools close, families who’ve chosen them during the enrollment window school will be contacted, IPS Superintendent Aleesia Johnson said. Johnson said the district sought to ensure that schools absorbing affected students would be able to accommodate them.

“Change of this magnitude is never easy,” Johnson said at the Tuesday agenda review session.

The proposed closures would be the most significant in the district since 2023, when IPS closed six schools in a bid to make the district more attractive to families while consolidating its operations. Other closures and consolidations happened in 2008 and 2017.

The timing is also significant: The district is set to cede some control over its buildings in 2028 when the Indianapolis Public Education Corporation assumes responsibility for buildings and transportation in IPS and charter schools within its boundaries.

Under the proposal up for a board vote, the district would keep its enrollment zones and grade configurations intact, Johnson said. IPS families could choose a different school than the default options within their zone and still receive transportation.

A huge factor in the looming school closures is the steep slide in enrollment in IPS in the last several years, a trend occurring in districts across the country. The district has lost roughly a third of its enrollment over the past decade, and the number of students in IPS is now below 20,000. Over the same period, charters have expanded, and combined enrollment in independent charters and those in the district’s Innovation Network now exceeds enrollment in IPS-run schools.

Earlier this month, the school board gave the district the go-ahead to start planning school closures following this school year. Shortly after Election Day, IPS Superintendent Aleesia Johnson also said the district had to plan for closures, despite the success of a $95 million tax measure at the polls on Nov. 3 that would provide money for both district-run and charter schools. Even with the success of that ballot measure, the district said it had to close a budget gap with $20 million in cuts.

The process differs significantly from what occurred four years ago, when the district spent months gathering and considering public input from the public before the board in 2023 passed what IPS called the Rebuilding Stronger plan, which included the school closures.

Notably, two schools slated for closure this year — Frederick Douglass School 19 and Robert Lee Frost 106 — absorbed students from closed schools in 2023.

Johnson noted one factor in the closure timeline is that IPS has a brief window to sell the buildings while the district still controls its buildings and while the state’s $1 building law, which requires districts to offer unused school buildings to charter schools for $1, does not apply to IPS. The sale of these buildings will allow the district to generate needed revenue, she said.

The district has recently tried to reassert its authority in a couple of areas. It withdrew from the universal Enroll Indy system for local schools and now uses an enrollment platform run by PowerSchool, a move that angered charters that have also used Enroll Indy. And it is pushing to renegotiate its contracts with Innovation Network schools in order to reflect the true cost to the district of providing them with certain services, IPS leaders said.

But neither of those moves solve the broader challenges that are pushing the district towards closures.

This story was originally published by Chalkbeat, a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.

item.title: Student Success and Public Trust
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed

The wisdom of crisis communications says: “If you’re explaining, you’re losing.” In the crisis of lost public trust in higher ed, too many institutions are explaining. Colleges defend their value with broad claims about lifetime earnings and graduate success. By offering counterpoints to critics, they validate the claims that college isn’t worthwhile, and their defenses fall flat with the millions of stopped out students for whom higher ed’s promises were broken. Instead of attempts to “change the narrative,” colleges need to prove that higher education is worth students’ time and money. Student success initiatives are perhaps the strongest piece of evidence colleges have to show they care about students’ futures.

At Inside Higher Ed’s annual Student Success US conference in Salt Lake City this week, a few things became apparent: Student success leaders clearly see students’ unique needs and learning goals. These administrators are not shy about naming higher ed’s failures to support students. They own those shortcomings and, despite thin staffing and minimal funds, their departments persist in coming up with new ways to address them.

The student success leaders in Utah told hard truths. They acknowledged that many of their institutions aren’t designed with students’ needs in mind—support services are only available from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; disjointed points of service have students running laps around campus, from the bursar to the financial aid office, to get answers to urgent questions. Institutions send too many emails, issue too many surveys and don’t use data effectively, administrators said. Faculty are often not included in student success conversations, they observed. Leaders grieved the students who drop out after the first semester when they can’t pay their first tuition bill.

But at the event, these admissions came paired with solutions, however small. The director of basic needs at a large public university found that 90 percent of students who received emergency aid enrolled in the next semester. Of those who got no aid, just 20 percent persisted. Committed to keeping more students enrolled, she launched a fundraising campaign specifically for emergency funds.

This is one example of how institutions are trying to support students with interventions. Others target food insecurity and meeting students’ housing and childcare needs. Complete College America (CCA) this week published a basic needs support guide for the growing number of institutions—from community colleges to large research universities— developing these programs. Meeting students’ basic needs is “the next frontier of the completion agenda,” Yolanda Watson Spiva, president of CCA, said in a release about the report. “Successfully addressing these needs ensures that students with increasingly diverse ages, work experiences and family responsibilities can find a path to and through college.”

Basic needs interventions are just one way student success administrators are helping students get through college. Others described their tactics for untangling institutional bureaucracies for students. When the University of Utah, our event host, identified gaps in how students navigate campus services, its student success leaders worked with students and staff to develop Answer U, a student support system that connects learners to career coaching, financial aid and scholarships, and academic advising. Mitzi Montoya, the university’s provost and executive vice president for academic affairs, said the system saves students from going from office to office to get information. Students’ questions also give her team real-time information on what they’re struggling with. “[We] understand where we need to redesign systems and processes because the answers are not easy to find,” she said at the conference. “And we now have a whole series of other projects related to it.”

Administrators also recognized that support services must adapt to students’ unique needs and learning goals. Academic advising for an 18-year-old is different from what a returning adult student needs, for example. And while lawmakers might equate higher ed’s value with graduate jobs and salaries, data from 55,000 students in the National Survey of Student Engagement’s (NSSE) Career & Workforce Module undercuts those assumptions. Students ranked expected job salary and availability fourth among the items that influence their career plans. Both first year and senior students said the factors that influence their career plans more are: Finding a job that fits their interests and abilities; a desire to make a difference in their community; and wanting to make an impact on society. Jillian Kinzie, associate director of the Indiana University Center for Postsecondary Research and the NSSE Institute, said the findings are a “serious” indication that students’ career goals are driven by their passions and desire to make a difference. “Two things to keep top of mind [for higher ed institutions] are: What are students looking for? And then, how are we going to communicate our larger responsibility to ensure employment and earnings together?” Kinzie told administrators.

Despite the initiatives and energy on display this week, student success can only go so far. Many of the problems contributing to America’s declining opinion about higher education require more systemic change. Colleges and universities are still perceived as too expensive and too many institutions are not transparent about cost. In our recent Student Voice survey of more than 5,000 students, just a quarter were highly confident their college or university is taking meaningful steps toward affordability, such as reducing unnecessary costs, limiting tuition increases or pooling resources. And just 29 percent fully grasp the total cost of attendance, beyond tuition. Student success leaders can’t communicate the impact of academic research or protect the public funding needed to sustain it, either. And while they can create mentoring programs to help students maintain academic momentum and provide teaching and learning training to faculty, student success leaders can’t change academic incentive structures that reward research over teaching, or control whether a curriculum is relevant to employers.

A first step to rebuild trust in higher education is admitting that too many students fall through the cracks—a reality the student success leaders readily acknowledged in Utah this week. As those administrators return to their campuses with new ideas and renewed energy for their work, I hope they have the full support of their institutions. Student success leaders can spearhead initiatives that show a skeptical public that colleges want their students to thrive, but they can’t do it alone.

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-20 08:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/opinion/columns/editors-note/2026/11/20/student-success-and-public-trust

item.title: ‘HBCUs Create Leaders’: America’s First Black Woman Governor is Florida A&M Alum
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Megan Varner/Getty Images

Georgia Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms campaigned on cutting healthcare and housing costs, making communities safer, improving K-12 schools and offering free community and technical college tuition. Throughout her 18-month-long campaign, Bottoms, a Democrat, rarely mentioned her identity as a Black woman seeking the top state office.

On Nov. 3, Bottoms became the first Black woman in the country to be elected governor. She will be sworn in in her hometown of Atlanta in January. Although she downplayed her background on the campaign trail, Bottoms’s identity—and her roots at Florida A&M University, an HBCU— matter deeply to people across the world of higher education, who see her victory as a powerful message to Black students and an affirmation of the enduring value of America’s historically Black colleges and universities.

Tashni-Ann Dubroy, chief business officer at the United Negro College Fund (UNCF), said it makes sense that Bottoms might want to de-couple her identity from her ability to lead, but her historic win is very much worth celebrating.

“I hope it really encourages our students to be considerably more ambitious in how they envision their futures,” Dubroy said. “There’s no need for them to qualify their aspirations because of the institutions they’ve attended. As a matter of fact, I think that those institutions give them even more credibility and grit to be able to ascend in positions of influence and to choose to do good with the influence once it has been entrusted to them.”

Bottoms’s win is also a testament to the value of an HBCU education, Dubroy said.

Dubroy is proud of HBCU alumni who “continue to raise the bar and excel,” she said, referring not just to Bottoms but to other HBCU alumni who also won at the polls. “Too often, we spend time trying to justify the value and we were asked so many times, ‘Are HBCUs still relevant?’ That question in and of itself is irrelevant.”

Bottoms’s alma mater, Florida A&M in Tallahassee, is the fifth largest HBCU in the nation, with about 8,500 undergraduates, according to federal data. It’s known for educating students in science, technology and health fields.

“Attending Florida A&M University was one of the most defining and rewarding experiences of my life,” Bottoms said in a written statement to Inside Higher Ed.

The FAMU community was large enough to help her grow and small enough to make sure she was nurtured and mentored, she said.

“I often think back to a lesson from my journalism professor, who taught me that there are no shortcuts to excellence,” Bottoms said in the statement. “He challenged me to understand the importance of putting in the work, even when it is difficult. That lesson has stayed with me throughout my career and reflects the kind of foundation FAMU provides in preparing students to become disciplined, driven leaders.”

Bottoms’s victory coincides with what leaders have identified as an HBCU renaissance. The last decade or so has been marked by significant philanthropic gifts, and excitement stirred by notable alumni such as former Vice President Kamala Harris, celebrity attention, and most recently, a Netflix reboot of the 1987 sitcom “A Different World.” For many historically Black colleges, this has resulted in growing interest and enrollment, even as many predominantly white institutions struggle to enroll students. At the same time, it helps fuel devotion among HBCU alumni, who, among other things, show up for homecoming in a big way.

Michael L. Lomax, president of UNCF, said that Bottoms and other newly elected state leaders who are proud HBCU alumni will only contribute to the mounting enthusiasm.

“I think that you’re going to see an even bigger surge in applications to HBCUs next year,” Lomax said. “You’re going to see a new generation of young people who are applying to college saying, ‘I’m not sure I like the way the world’s operating and I want to change it. Where’s the best place for me to go to become a leader?’”

They will turn to HBCUs, he predicted, because “that’s what HBCUs do, HBCUs create leaders.” Bottoms’s political ascent is a stunning example of that, he said.

Marva B. Johnson, FAMU’s president, said in a statement that Bottoms demonstrates that “leadership grounded in courage, conviction and a commitment to service can break barriers and inspire generations.”

“FAMU’s mission is grounded in our 1890 land-grant designation to open doors that were closed to too many, and her achievement shows what our students can accomplish when they walk through those doors with the academic foundation, leadership development and spirit of service they gain here,” Johnson said in a statement. Demonstrating the power of pride over politics, Johnson also celebrated the win of Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds, a Republican, who attended FAMU for three years before transferring to another institution.

‘Destined to Do Great Things’

Alan Williams, the university’s assistant vice president for alumni affairs and university advancement who was a few years behind Bottoms in school, said he followed her career as she served as Atlanta City Council member, mayor of Atlanta, and a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden.

“We knew that she was destined to do great things and have impact and have legacy—that is the DNA of FAMU alum,” Williams said. “HBCUs, not only do they encourage that, it’s almost a rite of passage to make sure that you go out and make the world a better place.”

Keneshia Grant, a FAMU graduate, said the sense of responsibility to make change was particularly acute at FAMU because of its proximity to the state capitol.

“You have an educational experience that is supplemented by your classmates and the notion that students should be active in the community as well,” said Grant, who is now a political science professor at Howard University.

Bottoms’s sense of duty may also have gotten a boost from her participation in FAMU’s Beta Alpha chapter of the Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc., a sorority that asks students to make a lifelong commitment to public service, Grant said.

For Grant, Bottoms’s ascent is, “amazing and heartwarming,” because it represents what those values can become.

Now, in her capacity as a political science professor at Howard, Grant said, “I write about Black people and demographic shifts and how they shape politics, so intellectually I understood that we were close but it’s a different thing to be living in.”

The governor-elect’s name itself holds a special significance, she said.

“People of my generation worry about our names, you know my name is Keneshia, and worry about whether these names prevent us from success in various arenas and yet we have the first Black woman governor in the nation whose name is Keisha,” she said.

The day after the election, Grant wore a Delta Sigma Theta shirt to teach her state and local government class at Howard.

Her students, she said, “saw themselves in her win with this idea that … if a girl named Keisha from Atlanta can be the governor, who knows what I could possibly do?”

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-20 08:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/government/politics-elections/2026/11/20/americas-first-black-woman-governor-florida-am-alumna

item.title: Burnham rejects calls for devolution of powers in letter to Welsh FM
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Burnham rejects calls for devolution of powers in letter to Welsh FM

- Published

The prime minister has rejected long-standing calls from the first minister of Wales for certain powers to be transferred from Westminster to Cardiff.

In a letter to Rhun ap Iorwerth, Andy Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve responsibilities over policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

The first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution" and not viewing Wales as an "equal nation".

Burnham's position is also at odds with Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates who reiterated his position at a party conference last weekend that policing and the Crown Estate should be devolved.

The letter, seen by BBC Wales, follows what had been seen as positive talks between the prime minister and first minister in Glasgow last month.

Asked about the prime minister's position on devolving policing following that meeting, ap Iorwerth said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there."

Burnham had also previously said he was "open" to the idea.

However, in his letter on Friday, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case.

"The integrated England and Wales policing system is essential to maintaining interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border working and ensuring forces in Wales can draw on national and specialist capabilities," Burnham said.

"Retaining that integrated framework helps ensure policing in Wales can respond effectively to threats and to protecting the public," he added.

On justice, Burnham said he "strongly believes" that the current devolution settlement enables Wales to "benefit from the resources, expertise and resilience" of a shared justice system.

"Effective partnership working is therefore essential to improving outcomes for victims, reducing reoffending and building safer communities."

The Crown Estate includes the seabed off the Welsh coast.

The land belongs to the reigning monarch, and the revenue from its property portfolio goes directly to the UK Treasury.

The previous Welsh Labour government as well as the current Plaid Cymru administration have long called for it to be devolved.

The prime minister told members of his party last week that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.

However, in his letter Burnham said the Crown Estate's "current model provides the best means of maximising the economic and social benefits for Wales".

He went on to say the UK government is "not persuaded by the case for devolving the management of the Crown Estate in Wales, nor to prepare for a future transfer".

Finally, on rail infrastructure, Burnham told the first minister: "I believe funding and delivery of infrastructure is best done by the new Great British Railways, in collaboration with Transport for Wales and Welsh government.

"I am therefore not persuaded by the case for full devolution of rail infrastructure, as it would fragment the current system and affect the service provided to the public by the highly integrated cross border network."

A spokesperson for the first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution".

"His warm words on devolution are now ringing hollow and there is no longer any doubt that when he talks of driving power out of Whitehall, he only means to the regions of England," they said.

The spokesperson added that Burnham's "refusal to even explore the devolution of the Crown Estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation."

item.title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company.

“Dear, dear Andy,” said António. “Dearest Andy, my adored Andy,” added Ursula. Neither could quite get enough of the prime minister. Andy fluttered his eyelashes bashfully. The feeling was mutual. It was hard not to feel a little bit sorry for Keir Starmer at this point. The deal that was being agreed was basically the one he had spent much of his last year in office negotiating. Now he had been totally airbrushed out of history.

It wasn’t all about Andy’s devastating good looks, mind. Though the physical chemistry was unmistakable, there had always been something a bit reserved about Keir. Withholding even. Starmer always had one eye on Reform and was wary about starting a new relationship with the EU. He had too much of the uptight Brit in him.

Andy was far more passionate. Spontaneous. No qualms about stating the obvious that Brexit had been a disaster for the UK and he was keen to experiment with closer ties. Fair to say, the EU have always preferred to negotiate with someone who isn’t afraid to rush in. This wasn’t to be just a one-night stand. This could be the start of something lasting. Once everyone had done with their trust issues.

Costa went first. We were as one. Andy was always welcome in the EU. Mi casa, su casa. We want the closest possible relationship. We were hurt when you ditched us in 2016 and we are ready to love again – if a little circumspect. Even in a throuple, there are rules that must be observed. Von der Leyen was even more open. This could be the start of something big. Not just dinner – waffle had been on the menu. It was the most perfect night: youth mobility, food standards and trading emissions today. AI and defence tomorrow.

Then it was over to Andy. He made no apologies for his rapture. His was the love that dared to speak its name. This was a win-win for everyone. Good for Britain, good for Europe. Three-quarters of Brits wanted closer ties with Europe and he would try to make that happen. This was the love affair that would make the country £17bn better off.

The questions from the media almost felt like an intrusion on the burning passion of first love. Could they clear up one thing? Would the deal on youth mobility and red tape be dependent on agreeing tuition fees for EU students? It didn’t seem entirely clear …

“There is absolutely no confusion,” said Burnham. Laughter broke out in the media room. Andy looked hurt. No one likes people making fun of them when they are in the first bloom of love. Andy thought everything had been agreed; António and Ursula thought there were some finishing touches to be made. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. We seemed to have heard this one before.

Finally, the question we all wanted an answer to. Was this the limit that could be reached with an incremental approach? Or was now the time to think about formalising a new long-term relationship? With one voice they all expressed the desire that this was the start of something big. Something permanent. None of them were the same as they had been in 2016. Time to start again. With that they rushed to embrace one another. Were they wedding bells chiming in the distance?

But there are always some who can’t stand the sight of other people’s happiness. Former lovers. Those who aren’t even allowed inside the EU’s headquarters in Brussels because they are the only former MEP to be refused a legacy pass. Step forward, Nigel Farage. Just hours after the throuple had left the media centre to peel grapes for one another, Nige was standing in front of a wobbly camera to trash the new romance.

“I had never seen Burnham look so tense and shifty,” he said. Which was weird. Because the rest of the world had seen unadulterated happiness on his face. A man who had waited 10 years for this moment. But if Nige is miserable, the rest of us have to be too. The same with the Tories. They couldn’t quite say why they hated the new relationship but they just knew they did. The only pleasure to be had was in creating division and discontent. Divorce their only language of love.

So Nige reinvented reality to suit himself. Andy had directly reneged on the Labour manifesto. Completely untrue. This wasn’t a reset but an overturn of the relationship. Three-quarters of the country might want what’s on offer, but three-quarters of the country were being fooled. With the youth mobility scheme we were back to open borders. Almost as if Nige was deliberately making things up. Visas will still be required.

What really stuck in Nige’s throat, though, was Burnham calling this a moment of hope. Nige only trades in grievance and despair. No Brit should ever consider a relationship with a foreigner because no foreigners can be trusted. Best to stay single and unhappy. As so often, it sounded as though the person he was really talking about was himself. Forever the bridesmaid, never the bride.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-20 18:53 UTC

item.title: A Moment of New Hope for the Rohingya Community
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

On November 19, the United Nations’ highest court delivered a landmark judgment, finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Nine years after fleeing genocide in Myanmar, over a million Rohingya refugees continue to live in the overcrowded refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. For the Rohingya, the ruling issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) was a historic day. It marked a moment of new hope in their long-waited struggle for recognition, accountability, and justice. It also brought a new surge of hope about finally returning home – something every Rohingya dreams of.

“When I was watching the first public hearing in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar from a tarpaulin shelter in 2019, I was very hopeful for justice. But since it took time and the situation got worse day by day, I thought justice had died,” Ro Anis Ahmed, executive director of Center for Social Development (CSD), told The Diplomat.

“Today, I feel that justice is still alive. The ICJ’s judgment in favor of The Gambia is a historic legal victory for us, but the real victory depends on its implementation.”

The ICJ accepted the estimate that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2017 military operations, and found at least 1,834 acts of rape. About 750 people were killed in Min Gyi (Tula Toli), 358 in Chut Pyin (including 127 children aged five or under), and at least 82 in Maung Nu. The court said the Chut Pyin figures could not be confirmed but are believable. It also examined seven other sites of serious violence, and found that Myanmar destroyed Rohingya villages in a planned way and later built security bases and other infrastructure on the land.

According to a report by MSF, over 700,000 Rohingya were driven out of Myanmar within a few weeks in 2017. The military’s atrocities – including murder, rape, and arson – forced Rohingya civilians to flee their homeland and seek refuge in Bangladesh.

The ICJ case, which began in 2019, has drawn international attention because the Myanmar military has now been officially found guilty of genocide against the Rohingya – the first time a state has been censured under the U.N. Genocide Convention.

Human rights organizations and U.N. reports documented widespread mass killings, brutal sexual violence and gang rapes, torture, and the systematic burning of entire Rohingya villages in 2017. There was no single, specific reason behind the military’s targeting of the Rohingya; rather, it was rooted in racism, discrimination, ethnic differences, and religious distinctions.

After the military launched its brutal crackdown, many Rohingya fled on foot through forests and hills, while others crossed the Naf River in small boats. Some spent more than a week walking to reach Bangladesh. Most of them entered through the Naf River in Teknaf. During that time, many lost family members, homes, and all their belongings; others perished attempting to cross the Naf River after their boats capsized.

Some Rohingya attempted to reach Malaysia and other neighboring countries by fishing boat, but many of these individuals have since gone missing.

Those who fled to Bangladesh in 2017 are living in dire conditions today, while those who managed to reach Malaysia are hiding to survive due to brutal treatment from the government. Meanwhile, the Rohingya remaining in Myanmar’s Rakhine State continue to face similar forms of persecution at the hands of the Arakan Army.

“The [ICJ’s] long overdue verdict is in our favor, but our plight is not over,” said Sirajul Islam, a Rohingya poet and writer. “Our plight and quest for justice ends when our hope for home translates into reality.”

On November 20, the day following the ICJ’s ruling on the genocide case, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, Bangladesh’s foreign minister as well as the president of the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly, arrived with his delegation and other high-ranking officials from U.N. agencies and government in the Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar. They came to meet with Rohingya refugees and listen to their voices following the historic judgment.

A large gathering took place at Camp 4 football field, where Rohingya refugees had the opportunity to speak with the president of the U.N. General Assembly. During this visit, Rahman engaged with members of the Rohingya community to hear directly about their concerns and expectations.

The Rohingya community was overjoyed to see him back at the camp, as evidenced by banners adorned with his face. During his visit, Rahman stated that the Rohingya crisis is now a matter for the international community, and that the international community would work to address it as soon as possible. He expressed hope that the Rohingya would soon be able to return to their homes.

Rahman assured the refugees that he would return to the camp before long, bringing some good news.

This visit comes at a highly significant moment for the Rohingya community. While Myanmar remains a deeply hostile environment for Rohingya, international funding has caused drastic cuts to food and health care for the refugees.

Now the ICJ ruling opens a crucial opportunity in their pursuit of justice and a means to ensure their voices are heard. This ruling can’t give back the loved ones they lost, nor can it erase their memories. But it offers the community a new hope that justice is indeed possible. It is a historic moment for the Rohingya.

Enous Juhar, a Rohingya survivor of the 2017 violence, was forced to flee his home in Myanmar after the military’s brutal operations. He described his emotions after hearing the ruling: “Although I have lost my home and everything I had in my homeland, I remain hopeful today that justice is nearer, those responsible will be held accountable, and our suffering will be acknowledged, while also creating the path for our return to our own land by ensuring our safety, rights, and citizenship.”

Human rights activists have welcomed this ruling and are calling for concrete steps to be taken to ensure accountability, bring perpetrators to justice, and safeguard the rights and future of the Rohingya population.

For the Rohingya, justice would mean acknowledging their suffering, establishing accountability, and ensuring that such crimes never happen again and no criminal goes unpunished. But more than that, they also dream of a future where every Rohingya can live without fear and return to their homeland.

“The Myanmar military killed my father in 2017. Even now without my father, we continue to suffer in the camp,” said Amir Hossain, a 50-year-old Rohingya refugee. “Now all we want is to return home with full rights, safety, and citizenship.”

While survivors continue to carry the trauma of that violence, young Rohingya are growing up in refugee camps having never had the chance to set their feet on the soil of their homeland. Many young people have spent a significant portion of their lives in camps, where they face severe restrictions on freedom of movement and other basic rights. With a lack of higher education, there are limited opportunities for Rohingya youth.

In April 2026, the World Food Program (WFP) was forced to further reduce already limited rations. Consequently, some Rohingya refugees, particularly the youth, are engaging in criminal activities to survive. The elderly and children suffer from malnutrition and families struggle to sustain themselves.

For Rohingya refugees, pursuing justice is deeply linked not only to the suffering of the past but also to their future.

The Rohingya community’s message is clear: They have waited too long. Nine years is more than enough. They are not asking for sympathy; they are asking for justice. They don’t want to see another generation growing in the camp. All they want is to return home, but the return must be safe with full rights, citizenship, and dignity.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 18:20 UTC

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/a-moment-of-new-hope-for-the-rohingya-community/

item.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

Mr Burnham is on to something: polls consistently show that many voters think that Brexit has not worked out well and rejoining the bloc has gained popularity. The rise of the European radical right also probably changes the EU’s calculation about Britain. Building closer ties with a broadly pro-European British government could mean the terms of future agreements allow for Britain’s preferential access to the bloc. However, Brussels won’t offer something for nothing. As the Swiss ambassador to the UK told a Lords committee earlier this year: “If you want to have access to the common market, you will need to pay some cohesion money.”

Horse-trading is a feature of geopolitical life for Brexit Britain. The EU is using public borrowing and procurement rules to encourage defence production within Europe, create economies of scale and strengthen European supply chains. Britain balked at the financial contrib

ution Brussels wanted in order to join up. With British defence manufacturers in danger of losing access to an expanding European market, both sides have made noises about getting around the table – but so far a deal remains elusive.

Brussels’ “Made in Europe” industrial strategy poses another challenge. Britain imports cheap Chinese electric vehicles while the EU seeks to protect its producers. British carmakers, however, depend on European demand. Under proposals advanced before this meeting they risked being shut out of the market. The summit recognised this danger, promising closer cooperation on electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require Britain to align its policies with Brussels – without having a vote over them.

This week Labour’s Stella Creasy, and Bernd Lange, a senior German MEP, proposed a Swiss-style deal to restore Britain’s economic and diplomatic influence without rejoining the EU. But greater market access without membership means accepting rules that Britain cannot influence. Mr Burnham’s reset pursued selective agreements – allowing Brussels to press for concessions. Switzerland offers a warning: frustrated by more than 120 bilateral deals, the EU insisted on a new framework. Down the line, Britain could face the same dilemma. Mr Burnham must calculate how long the country can negotiate the benefits of membership without confronting the costs of staying outside.

item.title: Russia’s Changing Positions on North Korea Sanctions and Denuclearization
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

In recent years, Moscow’s official stance on North Korea’s denuclearization and sanctions has shifted: Russian diplomats now say denuclearization has become an irrelevant term and sanctions have proved ineffective. Both issues became part of Russia’s broader criticism of the United States’ policy.

Moscow’s skepticism of sanctions dates back to the 2000s. During the Six-Party Talks in 2003-2009, Russia argued that sanctions should persuade North Korea to maintain dialogue rather than punish it. After Pyongyang announced its exit from the Six-Party Talks in April 2009, Russia’s then-Vice Foreign Minister Alexey Borodavkin claimed participants would be better off discussing how to resume the multilateral format than strengthening sanctions.

When United Nations sanctions were tightened following North Korea’s second nuclear test in May 2010, Russia’s permanent representatives to the U.N. highlighted that the measures should not have negative humanitarian consequences and could be reversed if Pyongyang followed the resolution’s recommendations.

The sanctions regime on North Korea intensified in the 2010s, coinciding with the gradual deterioration of Russia–U.S. relations and Western countries’ introduction of sanctions on Russia. North Korea’s case was utilized to challenge the legitimacy of unilateral sanctions and the U.S.-initiated U.N. sanctions, as Russia’s Foreign Ministry and U.N. representatives began framing them as excessive and harmful to the humanitarian situation.

In 2017, Russian diplomats argued that sanctions did not achieve their security goal and caused a deterioration of living conditions in North Korea. While voicing concerns about sanctions’ effects, however, Russia still voted for their introduction, likely weighing China’s frustration with North Korea.

Relations with the United States and European countries deteriorated sharply since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and unilateral economic restrictions on Russia were imposed. Since then, Moscow has stepped up efforts to discredit Western sanctions.

After vetoing the resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts in 2024, Russia’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Vasily Nebenzya argued that the Panel of Experts’ work had been reduced to playing up to the West in recent years. Nebenzya claimed that North Korea’s legitimate activities had become a target of the Washington-led coalition’s pressure.

Given North Korea’s importance to China, Russia’s decision to veto the resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts in 2024 was likely coordinated with Chinese counterparts, rather than made unilaterally. Although the United States and its allies launched the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) to compensate for the loss of the Panel of Experts, Russia has stressed its illegitimacy, as it had no U.N. mandate. In 2026, Nebenzya claimed that MSMT’s reports were mere fabrications and disinformation.

The shifts in Russia’s official discourse on North Korea’s nuclear program are even more profound, evolving from firm condemnation of Pyongyang’s nuclear ambitions to acknowledgment of its self-defense measures as fully legitimate. A distinction should be made between North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs: while Moscow used to oppose Pyongyang’s nuclear tests, it never portrayed North Korean missile development as a threat. Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued protests each time North Korea conducted nuclear tests in 2006, 2009, 2013, 2016, and 2017. The statements consistently highlighted that these actions pose a serious threat to peace and security on the Korean Peninsula and across the Asia-Pacific region, with negative consequences for Pyongyang.

After signing the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership agreement, Russia’s official rhetoric on North Korea’s denuclearization changed. In September 2024, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stressed that it was a “closed issue” for Russia, highlighting that denuclearization had lost meaning given the intensifying South Korea-U.S. military alliance. Visiting North Korea in summer 2025, he stated that Russia respects Pyongyang’s actions and understands the reasons why it carries out its nuclear program. Lavrov explicitly cited the US and South Korea’s military exercises and the 2023 Washington Declaration that allowed Seoul to participate in information sharing and consultations regarding nuclear contingencies as an explanation for increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula.

Similarly, in November 2026, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova argued that Russia sees North Korea’s efforts to boost its defense capabilities “as entirely legitimate and justified, fully consistent with the right of self-defense enshrined in the U.N. Charter.” While this tacit acknowledgment of Pyongyang’s nuclear program challenges the NPT and the IAEA’s authority, Moscow frames its stance and North Korea’s policies as legitimate by selectively applying existing norms and interpreting international law in its own way.

Russia’s evolving approach to Pyongyang’s nuclear program and related sanctions is just one episode of its broader attempts to contest existing norms and challenge the United States’ foreign policy. It is also an example of Moscow’s effort to question the rules-based order, which it sees as imposed by Western countries without consideration of the interests of the Global South.

This line of criticism goes back to the late 2010s. In 2017, Lavrov argued that the West tries to replace the rule of law in international affairs with a rules-based order, suggesting that the Western interpretation of international law does not equal the law itself. As ambiguities in international law continue to expand and the international system becomes more polarized, more cases like North Korea may arise, where existing norms are contested.

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 17:58 UTC

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/russias-changing-positions-on-north-korea-sanctions-and-denuclearization/

item.title: These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is getting face unlock (but not Face ID)

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

Lock your iPhone Duo by closing it

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

Audio Intelligence

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

Siri AI app actions

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

The new Health app is back

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Fitness+ Gym Strength

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Siri AI can answer questions about an entire Safari page

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Safari gets vertical tabs

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Safari can now automatically turn websites dark

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

StandBy gets an upgrade

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

iPhone Duo gets Reachability

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Siri AI is available in new languages…

item.title: The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

How much does Amazon Prime cost?

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

All the benefits of Amazon Prime

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast, free shipping

- Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

- Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

- The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

- Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

- The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Deals, savings, and sales

- Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

- A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

- Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Medical care

- Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

- Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Streaming and digital perks

- Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

- Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

- Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

- Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

E-books and audiobooks

- Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

- Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.
